speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called I should like to bring to the notice of the house a matter which to me is of great importance.

Royal Seals
There appeared on the front page of an Ottawa newspaper yesterday the photograph of a young man, a servant of this house. No young man has his picture in the paper unless he has done something very good or something very bad. This young man on Sunday afternoon, all dressed in his Sunday clothes, with a companion, risked his life to save a little girl from drowning. The companion is Gordon Robillard, and the young man to whom I refer is Romeo Latreille. I would ask him to stand so that hon. members can look at him.
Romeo is a bashful boy, but he had initiative. He is a better baseball player than the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), and he may have saved a great star. I am sure that Romeo will keep an eye on her and encourage her, and no doubt, at some distant date, Romeo will take his little Juliet by the hand and remind her of April 18, 1939-

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO THE APPLICATION TO CANADA OF THE REGENCY ACT, 1937

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO THE APPLICATION TO CANADA OF THE REGENCY ACT, 1937
speechtext:
I wish to make a short statement,
which is not controversial, and on that to base several questions to the government, of which I gave notice yesterday.
The house will remember that Bill No. 76, dealing with the sealing of royal instruments, passed the house very rapidly on Tuesday afternoon last, the first day after the Easter recess. In accordance with the demands of the press that the progress of business be facilitated it passed without discussion, although I was absent and desired to put to the government certain questions regarding that bill upon its second reading or in committee- questions in which a considerable number of people in Canada who are interested in constitutional questions have shown deep concern.
The Regency Act, chapter 16 of the statutes of the United Kingdom for 1937, provides for a regency in the event of a sovereign acceding to the throne when under eighteen years of age, and that the royal functions shall in such case be performed in the name and on behalf of the sovereign by a regent. Provision is also made in the act for the appointment of a regent if, by reason of infirmity of mind or body, the sovereign is incapable for the time being of performing the royal functions, or is for some definite cause not available for the performance of those functions. The same act also provides that in the event of illness not amounting to such infirmity of mind or body, or of absence or of intended absence from the United Kingdom, the sovereign may, in order to prevent delay or difficulty in the dispatch of public business, by letters patent under the great seal, delegate to councillors of state, for the period of that illness or intended absence, such of the royal functions as may be specified in the letters patent.
It would appear that the Regency Act of 1937 probably binds Australia and New Zealand, as the parliament of neither of those dominions has yet adopted sections 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the statute of Westminster, 1931. although admittedly that statute does apply to Canada.
The Regency Act, 1937, as enacted at Westminster, does not recite that Canada has requested and consented to its enactment as provided in section 4 of the statute of Westminster, which enacts that-
4. No act of parliament of the United Kingdom, passed after the commencement of this
Royal Seals

act, shall extend, or be deemed to extend to a dominion as part of the law of that dominion, unless it is expressly declared in that act that the dominion has requested, and consented to the enactment thereof.
It is therefore possible that the Regency-Act, 1937, may not automatically extend to Canada as a part of the law of this dominion.
Several questions therefore arise for consideration :
1.	Will a regent, appointed under the Regency Act, ipso facto assume the performance of all royal functions relating to Canada, hitherto performed by his majesty in person?
2.	If not, why was not the necessary request made and consent given by Canada so that by its terms the Regency Act would apply to Canada?
3.	Is it assumed by the government that,
by the terms of the British North America Act, or otherwise, Canada now has the legislative authority to provide for the appointment of a regent in case the necessity should arise?	_
4.	What is now Canada's constitutional position in relation to the appointment of councillors of state under the terms of the Regency Act?
I am not requesting an immediate answer to these questions, but I respectfully suggest that at an early day and at a convenient time the government should clearly state the position which it officially takes with regard to these important matters.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO THE APPLICATION TO CANADA OF THE REGENCY ACT, 1937
speechtext: With regard to the remarks of my hon. friend as to his not being present when the bill concerning the sealing of royal instruments was discussed in the house, I may say that I did not know he intended to speak on that bill. However the matter is still before parliament in another place, and if my hon. friend has any objections I am sure he could see that they are registered before the bill becomes law. But I do not see the connection between that bill and the questions he has just asked. My hon. friend says he intended on the second reading of the bill to make the remarks he has made about the Regency Act and ask the questions which he has just put on Hansard. The two matters are independent of each other. However, I shall see to it that my hon. friend gets an answer to the questions he has just asked, except perhaps that as my hon. friend well knows, it is not the business or under the rules it is not the task of the government or the Minister of Justice to give what would purport to be legal advice. But there are questions of fact which are embodied in his query, and I shall try to meet his wishes as far as possible as soon as I can look into the matter.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I should like to direct the minister's attention to a statement he made the other day, appearing at page 2757 of Hansard. The minister was perturbed by statements made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), which statements he termed irresponsible. The minister had this to say:
Mr. Rogers:	I certainly do challenge the
figures, and I remind the hon. member that during the winter months there is not a province or municipality in which provision is not made for unemployed men.
Mr. Massey: For what time?
Mr. Rogers: From October until April.
Mr. Massey: For what class of men?
Mr. Rogers: Single unemployed men.
Would the minister care to elaborate on that statement? Surely he did not mean it exactly as it sounds?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I believe the statement as made represents fairly the situation that exists in all the provinces at this time. In British Columbia, to begin at the western extremity, provision is made for single unemployed men through forest conservation camps, and they are also granted relief during those winter months. In the western provinces provision is made under the farm employment plan, and in the eastern provinces from Ontario to Nova Scotia there has never been any exclusion of single unemployed men, who are eligible for any form of relief that may be given in those provinces. That relief is given largely through public works in a number of the provinces, and single unemployed men are eligible for it.
2894	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Surely the minister knows that there are young men in eastern Canada at the present time who cannot qualify for any form of assistance that is given by the provincial and municipal governments. Surely he knows that in the city of Ottawa, as in other cities of eastern Canada, young men who were shipped east from the camps of British Columbia do not possess the necessary residential qualifications to obtain relief in these municipalities. The minister must know that in this very city of Ottawa there are young men who were shipped east from British Columbia. Representations have been made to the city, to the provincial authorities and to his own department in their behalf. Some of those young men are still in this city. Some were successful in getting into the mission, where they receive two meals a day and a bed. Some cannot get a bed at all, because the mission is full. The minister must know that there are young men in the city of Ottawa at the present time sleeping in the union station and begging on the streets. When the minister makes the statement that adequate provision is made in every province and every municipality, it may be technically correct but it is a fact that there are young men, transients, for whom no provision is made. It seems to me the statement is misleading.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
My hon. friend has referred particularly to a group of unemployed young men who came to Ottawa some weeks ago from British Columbia. These men were formerly attached to a forest conservation camp in British Columbia known as the Cultus Lake camp. As the result of a violation of the discipline established in that camp two of the men were discharged and the remainder went on strike. The provincial government in charge of the administration of the camp then decided that it was impossible to continue the provision previously made for the men in the Cultus Lake camp, and they were offered transportation to their alleged homes in eastern Canada. I say "alleged homes" because, as the hon. member for Vancouver North mentioned last night, some of these young men did not have permanent domiciles here. At all events they were given transportation and also cash vouchers covering two weeks after arrival at their destination. Not many of these men gave Ottawa as their domicile; I think I am correct in saying that only two of them did so, but the entire group that was discharged from the Cultus Lake camp came to Ottawa. This was done, I suggest, not directly for the purpose of gaining employment, but, as some of their leaders have

acknowledged, for the purpose of bringing their condition to the attention of the dominion government.
I suggest to my hon. friend that if these men had obeyed camp regulations they would not be in the position in which they find themselves to-day. As the situation now stands they are eligible, equally with other single unemployed men in this province, for farm employment which normally develops at this time of year and also for such public construction projects as are undertaken at this time of year.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
When the minister makes statements such as this I wonder why he is surprised when vehement remarks are made from this side of the house. The minister is well aware that there is another side to the story. After all there were only 32 men involved in that incident at the Cultus Lake camp, but there are over two hundred of these men in the city of Ottawa to-day. There are men in eastern Canada who were shipped back from the Capilano Canyon camp, which was established in British Columbia for eastern transients. There are other men in eastern Canada who did technically observe all the regulations of the Cultus Lake camp but who were sent back east anyway. The minister says they were given provision for two weeks. All they actually received were two $4 cheques, and one of these had to be cashed on the way east because adequate provision was not made for food in all instances.
May I point out that the reason trouble developed in the Cultus Lake camp was that the men never got a break from the start. In the first instance they were kicked around the streets of Vancouver from the police station to Abbott House, back and forth, and an effort was made by the provincial and federal authorities to crush an organization which they had a legitimate right to form to bring their grievances to the attention of the government of the day.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What evidence has my hon. friend for that statement?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Evidence of actual contact, and experience with the situation in Vancouver. There has been almost daily contact with the men and daily negotiations by some of my colleagues with the authorities, seeking redress of the legitimate grievances of those men in Vancouver.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
The hon. member has stated that the federal and provincial governments were out to break up the organization. What evidence has he?

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I said breaking up a legitimate organization which was formed to bring their grievances to the attention of t'he public.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What evidence has he the federal government has done anything in that direction?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I said the authorities.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: You said the federal and provincial governments.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I said last night that the federal government never took any steps to aid 107 men who were sent to gaol and sentenced to four and six months at the time the agreements to establish the forestry camps were under consideration. Surely officials of the federal department knew that those agreements were in course of preparation. If they had advised the police authorities at Vancouver that these agreements were on the way, no man would have gone to gaol. Steps would have been taken to look after them in the interim. If that was not a fair indication of an attempt to crush their organization, I do not know what it was.
The transients who went to the camp were put on a forty-four hour week, with arduous manual labour, and were not allowed at the outset one cent of cash to put in their pockets. They were allowed goods to the amount of $1.25 per week, from the camp commissary. The camps were not in operation more than two or three weeks when the men were in trouble with regard to this grievance, and it became necessary, through cooperation with provincial authorities and others, to negotiate on behalf of the men. When the difficulties were brought to the attention of the provincial minister of labour they were quickly ironed out. But the minister of labour in British Columbia did agree that the men could establish within the camp their own organization, a cooperative committee which would have the right to approach camp authorities with regard to their legitimate grievances. The difficulty arose in Cultus Lake camp. It should be said in fairness to the men that there was a misunderstanding. The authorities could have exercised leniency. A great majority of the men did turn in an honest day's work, did try to abide by the rules, and did try to use legitimate legal channels in seeking an adjustment of their grievances. It is the denial to the men of the right to secure redress for legitimate grievances which has caused ninety per cent of the trouble to which the minister has referred.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It had not been my intention to enter into a discussion of this matter. But listening, as I have listened, to the
"observations of hon. members, and particularly hon. members belonging to the two groups directly opposite me, it has-

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Got to have some education of the members of the house.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Perhaps I can give you some education. But above all, what gets under my skin is this, that there is a deliberate attempt, as I see it, on the part of certain members to encourage our young Canadian men to rely wholly on the government for their livelihood.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What else can thej do?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
What else can they do? What did you and I do? Did you or I ever ask the government to help us out? I never did, and I do not know of any young man in my own community who was brought up to believe or to think for a minute that the government should be responsible for providing him with a living. We were brought up to believe that it was our right to live, and that it was on our own initiative that we must make a living. It was up to ourselves to do it.
When hon. members talk about single homeless transients I always think of the single homeless transients in my own community and in any other rural community throughout Canada. They are the young men, homeless young men who have come from the old country. Even in the hardest of times I have never known any of those boys to drift back to those communities when the doors were not opened to them. Some farmer was always ready to give them a job. Perhaps they would have to work at small wages; certainly the wages would be small in bad times, but they always had a home, and wages enough to provide them with clothing. They had food to eat and a place in which they could find shelter.
My suspicions of last summer, on a very hurried trip to the west, have been confirmed by the observations of the hon. member who has just taken his seat. While travelling on the train I did suspect that a definite organization had been formed among the men who termed themselves the single homeless transients, that they had their officials travelling from east to west organizing and disciplining them. Well, evidently that is true. Just what class of men are leading the organization is something I should like to know. During my brief stay in Vancouver I took occasion to look around and to inspect particularly the post office where the men sat down last spring.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
On what I considered good authority I was informed that a large percentage of the men who sat in the post office last year had prison records. Here is something-

On what
authority does the hon. member base that statement?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

Another ir-

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

Here is something else
which-

speechtext: He should withdraw that.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I had friends at Penticton. Naturally in travelling around one takes occasion to ask questions here and there about things in which he may be interested. Here is something I learned. In the summer months a body of 163 transients drifted into Penticton. What did they do? They went around to the authorities and asked where they were going to be billeted. The armouries, or some such building was turned over to them. They set up their own establishment and put out their own pickets. A policeman came around to look them over and was informed that he was not needed, that they were looking after themselves. They sent their publicity men around to the printing offices to have their literature printed, and that literature is sold here and there throughout the city. Naturally they pick up a lot of money in that way. Anyone would give them a dime or a quarter. That amount was in addition to what they were already getting. I have just forgotten the figure, but I believe they received S3.68 each for three days, or six days-something like that-to last them two weeks. However, here is the point I am making. I was talking to the man sent out to interview them and ask them to go out and fight forest fires-which were raging in British Columbia. Only 40 out of 163 would go, on government pay.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: How much?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Regular wages-I suppose it would be thirty-five cents an hour. However, the greater number would not go.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Based on gossip.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is not gossip. I was
talking to the very policeman who went to interview them. Then the hose were cut and sand was put in the gasoline, and that sort of thing.
When we listen to this talk we ought to remember we are not talking about ninety-five per cent of the splendid Canadian boys

who are finding their own way, and making their own living. We are talking about that five per cent who for some reason or another do not get work-and I am going to say this, that in my opinion some of them are transients by choice, and not because they have to be. Even if a boy did not know anything about farming, if he would go to many of the farmers in this country and show a willingness to work for what the farmer can afford to pay him for the time being, he would receive work, and in a year or two he would develop into a man who could go out and do any kind of hard work, and find a job. You do not go through any of our rural communities and find men looking for jobs. Jobs are waiting for them.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
May I ask the hon.
member a question?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
You listen; we have listened to you, plenty. We have not taken up a great deal of time, but we have heard plenty from you.
Let me give you this illustration. Perhaps you would term this man a single homeless transient. He is an old country boy, and he has been working for us on and off for a few years.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What did you pay him?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: We paid him a dollar a day and his board and lodging. On a Saturday night in August he quit his job of his own free will.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I do not blame him.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
He was what you might term a single homeless transient. What did he do? On Monday he went up to a lumber camp to work, at a rate of $37 a month with his board and lodging. After seven months he came back and he was able to fit himself out with a new suit of clothes, an overcoat, shoes, and all the rest of it. In a couple of days he started to work for us again at a dollar a day, and was quite satisfied and happy to do so. This is just an example of what is happening all over the country. These boys out in the country are not begging the government to keep them. They are getting out and finding their own jobs. Some of these boys have worked for $10 a month, and perhaps even less, but they are real men. This man I am talking about can go into a lumber camp and do the hardest work; he can turn his hand to anything. When this man quit on a Saturday, we hired another man on Monday who stayed with us two months. He was paid a dollar a day, but then he quit and found his way into the

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
lumber camps. He worked for five months at $37 a month. This country is full of that type of men. I suppose ninety-five per cent of our young Canadians are of that type; yet we have to listen here day after day and week after week to speeches which would indicate that the remaining five per cent are the only young Canadians who amount to anything, or who are of importance in this house.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: If conditions in Canada are such that any young Canadian who is willing can get a job, how is it that there are more native bom Canadians living in the United States than there are in Canada?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Our young Canadians are so capable that they can go to the United States and get jobs.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: That statement is not correct. Give us the figures.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I have never heard that statement contradicted before.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I dispute it and I defy the hon. member to prove it. The hon. member is making the statement; why should I prove it for him?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is a statement which I have never heard contradicted before. My own conclusion is that conditions here have been so mean in the past that more Canadians-
. Mr. McPHEE: Why did the hon. member come to Canada, then?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I was one of those who came here and stayed here, but there are more Canadians who have left this country to live in the United States than there are living in Canada.

speechtext:
Will the hon. member
answer this question? As he well knows, the leader of this group which has been forming in Ottawa is named Mason. Has Mr. Mason registered at the employment service in Ottawa since he arrived here two months ago?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I do not know. I have no knowledge of that fact.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Then I can inform my hon. friend that he has not. He arrived here two months ago, as my hon. friend says, presumably to look for work, but he has not registered at the employment service, or had not up until Saturday of last week.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The minister knows very well that the officials of the employment service are not encouraging men to register, and the men know very well that there is no hope of work.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
How can my hon. friend say that, when, as I informed him the other day, 1,300 men from the Ottawa office were placed
2898	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
on farms, last year, and they are now proceeding to farms at the rate of twenty-five per week?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I cannot answer as to
individual cases, but I do say that the great majority of these men have accepted work when it has been offered. They have been ready to take decent work at decent wages. Many of these men are without the proper clothes to permit them to work on a farm at this time of year, and they dare not accept such employment unless they are to be provided with clothes. Very few of them have proper shoes or warm clothing to permit them to work out of doors.
My hon. friend has suggested that the organization at the Cultus Lake camp was part of a dominion-wide organization, but when I visited there they had had no contact with any organization in any other part of the province. It was simply an organization formed to deal with their camp grievances, and to engage in mutually beneficial work among the transients across Canada. That Cultus Lake organization was not part of any organized scheme for subversive purposes, as was suggested by the hon. member.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: It looked as though there was some kind of organization when these men, after being turned out of the post office in Vancouver, went down the streets of that city and broke $30,000 worth of plate glass windows.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Since this matter has been brought up by a number of hon. members this afternoon, it is important that the record should be complete and not open to contradiction. The particular group to which my hon. friend has referred came to Ottawa from Cultus Lake.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: How many?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The nucleus of the organized group in Ottawa, numbering some thirty-two, came from the Cultus Lake conservation camp in British Columbia.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Some thirty-two?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The nucleus of the group. As a matter of fact there was no organization of single unemployed men in Ottawa until these men arrived here.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: That is not so.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
As I mentioned a few moments ago, these men were discharged from Cultus Lake camp because of a breach of the regulations. After their discharge an inquiry was addressed to the administrator of unemployment relief in Victoria by Mayor Telford of Vancouver, and the administrator of unem-

ployment relief, Mr. Griffith, replied in the following terms-I place this telegram on Hansard because it is a public document and sets out clearly what was done for these men in the forest conservation camps:
Mayor J. Lyle Telford,
City Hall,
Vancouver, B.C.
Your telegram eleventh to chief forester referred to me for answer. In dealing with transients from Ontario, Quebec and other eastern provinces who were not eligible for assistance in this province, it was decided that rather than ask them to make their own way home again we would provide them with work to enable each man to earn his railway fare home plus sufficient extra money to carry him for half month after arrival. Separate camps were established at Cultus lake and Capilano, but working conditions, food, shelter, recreation, et cetera, are exactly same as in all other camps. These men were provided with complete outfit of clothing and boots. They were allowed two fifty per week for personal commissary, half payable in cash, and provided with excellent food, recreation facilities, medical, dental and hospital care, and freedom to go where they pleased during non-working hours. Every man agreed to terms before entering camp, but from inception at least sixteen men have been determined to disorganize the camp and prevent others from working. In addition to malingering, destroying property and using obstructive tactics, they apparently alienated the sympathy of residents in the district, who appealed early in December to have them removed on the grounds they were a menace to the community and to property. Despite all this we have endeavoured in every way possible to persuade the men to obey camp regulations and do a reasonable day's work. On ninth instant two men failed to report for work and were dismissed, and on the tenth forty-seven men left their jobs and departed from camp. These men were not dismissed but could not be maintained in idleness in a work camp.
They went on strike, as I explained a moment ago.
No assistance will be afforded to them, but any individual applying for transportation will receive it immediately.
E. W. Griffith.
That is the statement made by Mr. Griffith to Mayor Telford of Vancouver.
I wish also to place on Hansard the official report of what took place at Cultus Lake which led to these men leaving that camp, returning to eastern Canada, and then concentrating in the city of Ottawa. This was the report:
About 2 p.m., Monday, January 9, a telephone call was received at the Victoria office from Mr. Carl Bloom, foreman in charge of project No. 19, Cultus Lake. Mr. Bloom informed us that three men had returned to camp at noon on that day to go to work. These men had not received and had not asked for permission to absent themselves from camp Monday morning; consequently immediately they returned they were discharged. The remainder of the men under the leadership of Harold W. Mason, a camp enrollee, intimated to the fore-

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
man they would go on strike if these three men were not reinstated. Upon further consideration, however, they decided to return to work and despatched Mason to phone the Victoria office to try and have Bloom's decision reversed.
Bloom was foreman of Cultus Lake camp
Mason phoned this office at approximately 3 p.m., Monday, January 9, and was told- after hearing his story which concurred entirely with Foreman Bloom's-that the foreman in charge of the camp had made a fair decision as far as this office was concerned and we would in no way reverse it. Mason's only reply was that he could not be responsible for the actions of the men in camp if the discharged trio were not reinstated.
At 10 a.m. Tuesday, January 10, a further telephone call was received from Foreman Bloom informing us that the majority of the camp were on strike and asked for further instructions. He was informed that the men would either have to go to work or leave camp immediately and was told to have the provincial police on hand in case of any demonstration. About 11 a.m. of the same day another phone call was received from Bloom informing us that 47 of the men in camp had packed their belongings and calmly walked out. This left 18 men in camp who refused to go on strike.
This insurrection culminated two months of concentrated efforts on the part of the camp enrollees to accomplish as little work as possible during working hours and to make life as miserable as possible for camp officials both during and after working hours. There is no doubt but that the main body of camp workers were dominated by a subversive element specially trained in the art of disorganization.
And yet my hon. friend accuses the federal and provincial governments of seeking to disorganize the camp. The real source of the disorganization is evident in the official report. It continues:
This subversive element consisted of the eighteen members, marked by asterisk, in the following list. Approximately thirty of the strikers left camp only through the influence of these 18 agitators. The thirty "lukewarm" strikers were possibly afraid of the consequences threatened by the agitators if they refused to take a strike action.
Personally I am glad the hon. member for Renfrew North has placed this problem before the house in its proper proportions.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Does the minister endorse his view?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Let me continue, if you please. From the very beginning I have expressed the view that the vast majority of the single unemployed men are ready and willing to work and deserve every reasonable assistance that can be given them. I submit, and I did say last year at the time of the Vancouver troubles, that the interest of the vast majority of these men has been prejudiced by the agitation of a limited few, whose interest is rather in the organization of the unemployed and their exploitation, and not,
I submit, in the welfare of that body at large. I suggest that it is wholly unreasonable to expect that any group of single unemployed men as a result of demonstration or organization, can be given preferred employment on public works-and I wonder sometimes if my hon. friends in that corner of the house still conceive of work in any other terms. They seem to assume that the only work available in this country is such as can be provided by governments. A certain amount of work is provided for these men eveiy summer by governments, through the expansion of normal services. We are this year expanding the normal services in forestry, which undoubtedly will have some effect in providing employment for this group of men. So far as the vast majority of them are concerned I have no doubt at all that they are ready to work. But the few who engage themselves in agitation, I submit, have very little claim on our sympathy.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Can the minister think of any industry in Canada that needs more men to-day? Can he think of one?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I can think of one, certainly. The basic industry of this country is agriculture.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: We cannot sell what we raise. We have to give it away.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I have already indicated that from this Ottawa office alone 1,300 men were placed on farms last year, and that is equally true of employment offices in other sections of this province. Farming operations begin at aibout this time of the year. If my hon. friends had their way, and if public employment were provided for all single unemployed men, I suggest that we would be doing a great disservice to the basic industry of this country.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The minister in reply to my question said that he could name one industry that needed men-agriculture. I know he cannot think of any other industry, because there is none where there is opportunity for further employment. How many single transients are there in Canada, and how many unemployed young people are there who are not transients but are living at home and being taken care of by their parents?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
So far as single transients are concerned for whom no provision whatever is made, the number certainly would be well under the ten thousand mark. That was the computation which was made as a result of an inquiry sent to the provinces earlier this winter. In the majority of the provinces- I include only those men who are really on the rolls-some provision is available during
2900	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
the winter months, and in some of the provinces that provision is extended through the summer months as well. Other provinces believe from experience that it is possible for these single unemployed men to find seasonal employment in the summer months. For that reason the relief measures are withdrawn, sometimes in the middle of April and sometimes the first of May. In British Columbia the period of seasonal employment is usually extended from June until October. Certainly, if my hon. friend is aware, as I presume he is, of the demand for agricultural assistance and for other forms of seasonal employment in western Canada, he will know that there is occasionally a month when the increase in employment offered in this country has reached as high as 60,000 to 75,000. I doubt whether there are many countries in the world where there is as large an incidence of seasonal employment.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The minister said there were about 10,000 single transients roaming up and down across the country, but I asked him for the total number. According to the dominion commissioner of unemployment relief, in his report for 1935, the persons actually in relief camps on March 30, 1935, were 20,359, while the total number who had passed through the defence camps at February, 1935, was 112,949. It has been estimated that there are about 400,000 single unemployed throughout Canada. I want to know whether the minister has the actual figures to show the number of single unemployed persons, those who are transient and those who are living at home, unemployed. Can he give me a complete picture of the youth problem?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: As regards the registration of those on relief, the figures are available, and I will secure them for the hon. member when the bill is before the committee. As regards the unemployed on relief, a census taken in 1936 in the western provinces gave some indication of the comparison between the young unemployed on relief and the unemployed not on relief. I had occasion to refer to these figures some time ago and I will look them up again and present them later.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Agriculture being the only industry that employs single unemployed men, I was naturally interested to find out what percentage of the unemployed could be employed in agriculture. It is seasonal employment. They pick fruit in eastern Canada and do some harvesting in the west in the fall and some work in the spring when the crops are going in, and they also do a little work in British Columbia. It is seasonal employment extending over four months of

the year altogether. In the fall and the spring together it is about four months. The committee that was discussing the youth problem with me stated that to-day there is no opportunity for employment in seasonal work in agriculture for more than between 35 and 40 per cent of all the available man power among the single unemployed. The minister should be able to give a complete picture of the youth problem. The hon. member for Renfrew North says that we are concerned only with five per cent; that is all we hear any talk about. Well, the minister cannot give us a complete picture of the situation. He is not in a position to give us the exact figures. Thousands of trained artisans, bricklayers, plasterers, plumbers, men in all walks of life, are unemployed, and they have no opportunity. I hope the minister will be able to give us all the figures setting out a complete picture of the youth problem in Canada. Are we to say that there is to be no opportunity of employment for these men in the years to come? Are we to say that all they can do is work on the farm for 85 a month, and for the rest of the year go from pillar to post, eating in slop kitchens or being put into relief camps, or being forced to draw attention to their plight by means of insurrection or the taking over of some government building, the government bombing them out with gas bombs, and chasing them back and forth? Is that to be the future of the youth of Canada? We want to know what opportunity there will be for them.
The government say, "We will put them in industry." But what opportunity is there for them in industry? Thousands of young men are coming out of schools and universities better prepared to make a contribution to the development of the country than was the hon. member for Renfrew North when he was their age, but no opportunity is afforded them. The future is closed to them so far as the development of this country is concerned
I should like the minister to review the whole situation and to hold out some hope for these young people who to-day are despondent. In my own constituency dozens of young fellows come to me and write letters telling of their condition. On my own street not five per cent of the young fellows between the ages of eighteen and twenty-five are employed. They cannot get jobs. Ask any man in any city and he will say he knows personally of ten or fifteen young fellows between the ages of eighteen and thirty who are unemployed. That is the position to-day, and every member knows it. It is true of my constituency and it is true of every other.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: They are waiting for the S25.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
What have you to
offer them? It is all very well to say that there are only five per cent that we have to worry about, but the problem is far more serious than that.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: It is unfortunate that a party should take up this cause in such an absurd way. We know there are some unemployed. There have always been and there will always be. The minister made the statement that seventy-five per cent of them are willing to work-

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Ninety-five per cent.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I have not found it so. I have farms lying idle and there are many farms in western Canada that are idle.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Why are they idle?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The trouble is, the young men to-day are lacking in spine.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: That is a slander.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yes, and you fellows are
encouraging them in a lot of nonsense. I have tried to get men time and again to work. I have one farm idle and I want someone to work it. I am offering to equip it and supply it with grain, and whoever works it can make half the profits, and I will give him part of the wages as he goes along.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: At sixty cents a bushel?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I have asked many men in the last two weeks to take the farm, but when I approach one capable looking fellow I find that there is beer on his breath. Then I try another fellow to see if his breath is free of beer. These fellows are out licking up beer and smoking cigarettes and I cannot have them around my barn smoking cigarettes. I try to pick out fellows who seem to have personality, but they will not work on my farm. I tried to get a brick house moved on one of my farms and I went to a bricklayer who was whining just as you fellows are, but he talks a lot of nonsense, because I found that he wanted 810 a day to lay 400 bricks.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What do you get?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I told him, "You had better go and lay bricks for yourself." I doubt if any of you have any hired men working for you. I doubt if any of you need a hired man, and I doubt if many of you are working yourselves. I go on the farm and I work with the men; I know and understand their troubles just as well as hon. members do.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I thought you said
you could not get any.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I have a large number of men working with me all the time, and I have sympathy with them. But when I go to your city bums from the street I cannot get a man in fifty. You might think you could, b.ut just you go and hire some of these yaps on the streets and you will see what you have got. In the country I can get men that have a spine but I cannot when I pick up these travelling transients. I give them rides up and down the road in my car-not as many of them as I did a few years ago; there are not so many-I question them: Do you want a job on the farm? They answer, no.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What do you pay them?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I am trying to come to
terms with them. If I were out of a job I would work for my board and clothes rather than beg.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: It is all right to say it now.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: These spineless fellows rambling about and depending on you to keep on doing it expect to be carried in an economic sedan chair and to be spoonfed. It is a strange picture.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Is that
the attitude of the Liberal party?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I am speaking of what I see myself, and I must say I do not like the attitude of the parties on that side. Do not encourage them to think that the government should carry them along; talk sense to these fellows, tell them to get a job for themselves, stand on their feet, be men.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Why did you not say that in 1935?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I always said it.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Quote what your
leader said in 1935.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Order. I would ask hon. members in the far corner not to interrupt the hon. member who has the floor.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: One in particular, interrupting all the time.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Our papers are full of war scare news, and it is destroying our industries. Those who are running our industries keep their money in the banks; there never was as much money in the banks as there is at the
2902	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
present day. The war scare is keeping our industries from going forward, and between the newspapers and the radio it has caused a lot of unemployment. What we need is to let this war scare die down. Our boys should be encouraged, and not told that we are going to carry them along and spoonfeed them. It destroys personality, destroys manhood. Tell them to get out and find work for themselves, not expect people to run to them with a job; if they cannot get one job, to get another. If we do this it will be better for all concerned.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Nothing has come to my attention during this udiole debate that has shown the lack of understanding on this question as clearly as the statement made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) a few moments ago in reply to the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou). The minister was asked where employment could be found at the present time, and he replied, in agriculture. As if increasing the number of people engaged in agriculture were going to get the people of this country out of any of their present difficulties! If you could put all the unemployed in Canada into agriculture, what would happen is that you would have to pay in bonuses to farmers and in set prices for wheat and butter and cheese and other agricultural products what you are to-day paying to the unemployed in the form of relief.

speechtext: Is not that your policy, to pay bonuses?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is not only our policy, it is your policy, but you do not admit it is your policy; you just carry it on because you do not know how to work out another policy. This lack of understanding is the more regrettable in a man of the intelligence of the Minister of Labour, who should have understanding. As I sat here and listened to his supporters in this debate I felt sure that he was caused more embarrassment by his supporters than by any criticism from this side of the house. We have hon. members standing in their places here, as happened the other day, and saying that we always had unemployment, that Christ said "Ye have the poor always with you," and another hon. member over here to-day saying that if we end unemployment we are going against what Christ said. What blasphemy! Although Christ did say "Ye have the poor always with you," it does not mean at all that there was unemployment in His time. All down through the ages there has been poverty, but that poverty is not the same as the poverty of to-day. The poverty of other days was poverty because of scarcity, because of the 
inability of people to produce from nature sufficient to feed themselves. But the poverty of to-day is caused by the ability of the people to produce too much. The poverty of the last eight years has been a poverty of abundance. Did not the Prime Minister state that very clearly on October 14, 1935 when he was elected? Let me read it again, so that hon. members can get it into their minds, get it so they will not forget it, and consequently so that they may have some clear idea of what is wrong in society to-day. He said:
We take up at once, as our supreme task, the endeavour-
Endeavour to do what?

to end poverty in the midst of plenty, starvation and unnecessary suffering in a land of abundance, discontent and distress in a country more blessed by Providence than any other on the face of the globe.
Those are the words of the Prime Minister, spoken when he was elected in 1935. That is what hon. gentlemen opposite blamed the former government for not doing, yet when the question comes before them to-day, what do they do? Man after man on that side of the house gets up and libels the young men of this country, the young men whom, if war were to break out to-morrow, they would call upon to defend the institutions of this country. What institutions are they to defend? Soup kitchens, camps, hostels, lousy dumps, all that sort of thing; that is all you have given them. Now, sir, that is not good enough. We want something better than that for the unemployed, and they are entitled to something better.
There is only one thing wrong with our economic life to-day: it is not properly organized. There is enough for everyone, but when I read in the press that a man died here a few days ago leaving a fortune of $6,000,000 I can understand mass poverty. I can understand mass poverty when we allow one individual to amass wealth to that extent. That sort of thing will have to be stopped before anything can be done with the problems confronting us to-day.
I have nothing but the most kindly feelings towards the Minister of Labour. I dislike immensely having to criticize him, because I know the difficulty of the task with which he is confronted, and I know also it must be distasteful to him to stand up and defend the policy that he has to defend. And I say again, it is distasteful to me to criticize him. But he says these men are interested only in organizing and agitating.

There was organization and agitation by the men at that time, and when they placed their case before the Minister of Labour he readily saw their position and made some concessions. Every time anything has been done, first of all there had to be a disturbance, a demonstration by the men to show that they were no longer prepared to put up with the conditions under which they were labouring. These are the things we must take into consideration.
I regret also that my hon. friend referred to Mason, who is the leader of the men who came here from British Columbia. I happen to know that Mason has been ill most of the time he has been here. A few of my friends gathered together enough money to engage a room for him, where he has been in bed for some little time. Then there is the further point, that the greater the number of unemployed the greater the uselessness of the labour exchanges. There is no use going to a labour exchange every day when you know there is nothing at that labour exchange for you.
I wish we could meet this situation fairly. I wish we could realize the plight of these men. I wish we could realize that they have hopes and aspirations and desires the same as we have. They see their hopes unrealized; they see their aspirations frustrated; they see their desires can never be fulfilled, and we must realize that when faced with difficulties of this kind men cannot be normal. They become anti-social. But they are what they are because society has made them so. We are responsible for what they have become; we are upholding a form of society that can no longer feed, clothe and shelter this great mass of people. I have stated time and again why that is so. Until we realize it and take steps to do the things we should do; until we realize that we are trustees for the people of this country and that we should get busy and arrange our economic and social organization so that we may take advantage of the
wealth of this nation, this condition will continue. I am not one of those who believe you can get something for nothing. I am quite satisfied that there is only one way of getting anything, and that is by working for it.

The abundance we produce is taken by somebody else, and when he passes away he leaves a fortune of 86,000,000, which he could not possibly obtain by means of his own labour, a fortune which he could accumulate only by appropriating the unpaid labour of others. And then the unpaid labourer walks the streets looking for something to do. I plead with the Minister of Labour to take a bold stand and refuse any longer to be a catspaw for a government that will not do anything, that will not fulfil the obligations it took upon itself in 1935. Hon. gentlemen opposite criticized the former government for not doing the very things we are asking them now to do; having had far better opportunities than the Conservative government ever had, they leave things in a worse condition than that in which they found them.

Let me go on. I happen to have in my pocket a letter which I have been carrying with me for two months. I expected to see the young chap who wrote this letter and I wanted to have it on hand if that happened. Perhaps it is a good thing I have it with me now. The hon. member for Wellington North referred to a great many of these young people as spineless creatures and so forth. Here is the letter, and I should like to give you the history of the young man who wrote it. He graduated from high school a few years ago and secured a position. He desired to better himself and obtained leave of absence-which ultimately meant his resignation-in order to take two years of college work to fit himself for something he had in mind. By the time he had completed that work the depression had come and he found that he could not get employment. What did he do? He took a business course, .and after he had completed it and had received high marks, he tried to get a position. Nothing came along. Then he took another course, tthis time a secretarial course, but still was 
unable to get any work. For the last two years he has been taking the youth training which has been given under the authority of the government. Still he cannot find employment. This young man is not of the most robust type and cannot very well work on a farm. He is certainly not one of the spineless characters referred to, and I believe his is a typical case. This is what he writes:
I have told you before that I am discouraged, not having anything worth living for. And so when spring comes I am going to leave home.
This young man is not a transient. He is living with his parents, if you please. He continues:
I am going down east, and I am going to wander and wander around until I get a job. God knows where I am going to land; I don't. What is more, I don't care where it is. I waited the whole year of 1938 with the hope of getting a position. But now that that hope has blown away, I have made up my mind to leave this city, never to return to it. It is true I have not a trade. I do not hope to get anywhere in this world.
That is the discouraged position of this young man.

I am so downhearted I cannot sit down to study anything worth while. I am sick of the lonely life I am living. Of course I know what is in the minds of hon. members. They say that is only one case. I know that as a general rule you can prove anything by citing a case. But I am going to suggest to hon. members that that case is typical of many.

I am going to suggest it is the duty of this government to adjust the' legislation of the country so as to give the young men and women a chance to earn a living. It can be done.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

speechtext: Yes, what is a government for, if it does not do that? On one or two occasions we have heard the very familiar passage from holy writ to the effect that "the poor ye always have with you". Let me suggest to hon. members that that statement was not made by the greatest teacher who ever came to this world to substantiate the arguments of a Liberal government to the effect that we should always expect the poor to be here. While that great teacher was the greatest prophet who ever lived, the Liberal party must be under the impression that in looking into the future He thought we would always have a Liberal government administering the affairs of this country. But may I suggest that the same holy writ in which that passage of scripture appears, and which is not in support of a system which keeps men poor-

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

But you are interpreting that statement to mean that we must expect always to have the poor with us, and that we must do nothing to help them. That is not the position. I am going to read another passage from holy writ. It is not often the bible is read in parliament, but I intend now to read from it, and refer particularly to a passage in the old testament wherein the greatest law giver of all was telling the people of a nation what would happen if its governmental authorities did not do the right thing. I turn back to the book of Deuteronomy, where it speaks of certain laws which must be put into practice. The fifteenth chapter commences with a description of the manner of the release of debt at the end of every period of seven years. And then the law giver goes on to say:
1.	At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release.
2.	And this is the manner of the release: Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the Lord's release.
3.	Of a foreigner thou mayest exact it again: but that which is thine with thy brother thine hand shall release;
And the next passage:
4.	To the end that there be no poor among you.
I am saying that that was told to the government of one of the greatest nations on earth. It was not a Liberal government that time.

But I am not going to do that. He spoke of governments and holy writ. Let me inform him that the social credit principles are just about as close to divine law as you can possibly get. The sooner parliament recognizes that, the sooner we get back to some of these divine laws, the better will this country be. Surely one of our divine laws is that the blessings that come from the bountiful hand of the creator should be adequately distributed through the nation. I submit that the duty of this government is to bring about an adjustment of legislation to enable that to be done. I hope we shall hear no more innuendoes and insinuations along this line.
This group stands for a glorious Canada. Who will dare to say that we cannot have a glorious nation with all the resources and manpower that we have, with all the brains that we have available, such as those possessed by the Minister of Labour? I compliment the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) upon raising one of the most significant points raised during the present session-that this government has the brains and organization available, and yet it cannot accomplish a thing. Why? Because it is functioning under a system which has become obsolete. The hon. member for Peace River made it quite evident that no group of men, no collection of brains, no organization, could accomplish the solution of this problem under the present system. The system must be changed, and we are here to advocate a new system. Those who have ears to hear, let them hear.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Unfortunately the debate has developed into something of an attack on and a defence of a certain group of young men. This afternoon a number of undeserved and unfair statements have been made which might be interpreted as applying to a large group, when in fact if there were any element of truth in them, they would apply only to a small minority. I think before we recount gossip picked up on the train or from various'people across the country we should remember that we have available an authoritative report in connection with this important problem. I hold in my hand the final report of the national employment commission which was submitted to the government on January 26, 1938, on page 88 of which the transient problem is fairly and fully outlined. While it is contrary to my usual practice, I think in view 
of the debate which has occurred I shall quote substantially from this part of the report. It reads:
Families or individuals not able to establish legal residence as now defined in the centre in which aid is sought should not necessarily be classified as "transient" or "wandering." The cause may be that a move has been made in genuine search for work; employment may not have lasted long enough to establish residence; the change may have been an endeavour to get back home or into a familiar neighbourhood again; ill-luck, sickness, or shortage of funds may have halted men or family short of their destination. Or, of course, the case may be one in which the inability to establish residence is directly due to wanderlust, or to an endeavour, on the part of the family unit particularly, to locate in an area with "better relief," or with less rigorous climatic or living conditions.
This is the important part.
The problem of non-residence occurs more widely among self-dependent men "on their own." Development of Canada's resources demands a large supply of vigorous, mobile labour. A shifting labour reserve, without definite residence, while aggravated in recent years by lack of opportunity for gainful occupation, is not only a natural but almost an essential feature of production in this country. Our great primary activities, along with closely allied secondary industries, employ almost half of the gainfully occupied population, the overwhelming percentage of whom are unskilled or semi-skilled wage earners. As such they are dependent for gainful occupation upon circumstances quite outside their own control. In many eases their occupations are seasonal and carried on in the isolation of frontier or "new" country. These men must move with employment demands, or lack of the same, and thus have not a free choice as to their place of residence. It is practically impossible for a man in this category to establish residence anywhere. Although he may have five or ten years' history of almost continuous employment it may be spread over widely different occupations in varying localities, one place in summer, another in winter, and so when idle, he keeps "moving on" in search of work, always hoping that somewhere the job he finds will last long enough to let him get settled.
The hon. member for Renfrew North refers to these men as transients from choice. The hard economic circumstances prevailing in Canada has made their transient life a necessity. The report goes on:
Thousands of these men have a legal residence claim somewhere, and the object should be to have this recognized and ensure "nonresident" families and men care on some reciprocal basis, and also that residence will not be lost in one place before being established in another.
To see what this problem really is in extent and nature, registration and classification is essential.
This recommendation was made over a year and a half ago.
Preliminary examination has shown that the difficulty in establishing legal residence is a greater factor in this migrancy problem than

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
any urge on the part of the men themselves to move on. It would also appear that well over one-half of these men are not "transients" in the accepted sense.
A little later on in the report the commission says:
In the depth of recent winters, this whole volume seems to have fluctuated between 85,000 and 100,000, where it stood in January of this year, including those placed on farms.
The commission then made certain recommendations, and I am going to ask the minister how many of these have been carried out. The recommendations were as follows:
1.	Establishment of definitions of residence on a comparable basis all across Canada.
2.	Reciprocal basis of maintenance and reimbursement among different units of administration in respect to those aided in a unit other than their own.
3.	Equitable apportionment of maintenance costs, and agreement on conditions for establishment of local residence for provincial and interprovincial residents and for migrants.
4.	Establishment of central bureaux for the "clearing" of non-resident and migrant applications in certain large centres of known concentration.
Those are the recommendations. There is the extent of the problem. The minister tells us that in his opinion there are this winter in the neighbourhood of ten thousand of these transients. But in a recent report submitted by one of the departments in the city of Vancouver it has been shown that this winter there have been, of one sort or another, some ten thousand transients dealt with in that city.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Surely not different transients. There must have been a repetition.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
There may have been some repetition; I could not say, because I did not see a breakdown of the figures. But in 1937, when conditions were admittedly better on the whole than they were in 1938, a commission set up by the government to inquire into this very problem states that including those on farms the volume seems to have fluctuated between 85,000 and 100,000 where it stood in January of that year.
To me the tragedy of this transient problem is not the momentary hardships. The tragedy lies in the ultimate effects of this situation upon the "future of the country in which we live. I was on a relief committee for a number of years. I was on it when the depression hit us in 1929. I served on it in 1931, 1932 and 1933, and I saw this happen: I saw men who in 1929 and 1930 would do anything and everything before they would apply for relief brought to the point where they had lost all hope and were permanently on the relief rolls.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: That does not apply to transients only.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No. I am saying I saw those men, and I have watched some of them for the last ten years. They were from forty to fifty when the depression struck, and ten years of enforced idleness has reduced them to such a condition that in my opinion they will never be fit to work again. Long years of relief have undermined them; long years of poverty have taken from them the ambition they once had. That is true of the group that is older than the group we are discussing. But we are doing the same thing to our young people. People who have now reached sixty have only another ten years before they reach the three score years and ten. Then they will pass beyond and no longer be a problem to us. But we have still these young men and these young women. I have seen them leave school-teaching was my profession before I came here-iboys whom I taught, went out into the world to look for something to do, and to-day they are moving across this country, hopelessly, almost aimlessly, seeking something that never turns up.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Would they not have homes?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: They had homes when you were teaching them.
