He did try to blast his way into the markets of the world; he did try to put into effect the policies in which he believed. I had no confidence in those policies. He perished in the attempt, as I felt he would. In 1935 the members of the Liberal party who to-day constitute the government of Canada said: "Return us to power and we will reopen the channels of trade, and end, or at least greatly alleviate, unemployment." But we are in the fourth session of this parliament, and unemployment is rampant right across this country, with misery everywhere. I say this to my hon. friends, as I have said before, that we must recognize, as the hon. member for Vancouver East told the house this afternoon, that this problem goes deeper, too deep to be cured by any of the palliatives that have been suggested. I am no revolutionary. I do not believe in the overthrow of our institutions or in any sudden changes overnight. I am not built that way. But I do say that we have to see the goal to which we are going if we are to take intelligent steps toward that goal, and then as we pass along we must institute policies of unemployment insurance, public works programs, and the like in order to alleviate conditions on the way.
In my opinion, this house should not think of prorogation, this house should not think of adjournment, until we have something far

more definite laid down with respect to two problems which were pressing in 1935 and which are still urgent, unemployment and the problem of agriculture. There is nothing that warrants this house in rising at the present time, or within the next month or two; for so far in four years this government has done nothing to meet the pressing problems which confront the country. I say, nothing, though I know my hon. friends opposite will point to the trade agreements. Well, I voted for both the trade agreements but I say they have done nothing to end unemployment. Nor could they.
In the resolution before the house there are one or two good things. The act to assist in the training of youth or the extension of youth training is in my opinion worthy of support. Most of us in this house probably have sons and daughters and I feel as the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) does when he says, "What are they going to do in a few years time?"

No, but I am suggesting that owing to the increase in productive capacity, owing to the advent of machinery, fewer and fewer people to-day are required to turn out more and more goods and that there are fewer jobs. That is true in agriculture and in every other walk of life, and we shall be faced with a serious problem until we meet these facts squarely and do several things which our group has suggested. We have suggested over and over again that men and women should be encouraged to retire from agriculture and industry before-the age of seventy; in other words, we have-suggested a lowering of the pensionable age and an increasing of the amount in order to encourage that retirement. We believe that in industry the hours of labour will have to be-controlled as well as the rates of wages. We must exercise some intelligence and not leave these things to chance. The day is coming when, if we do not do this, somebody will force us to do it. But there is a graver danger than that. I have met young men who-have said to me, "Well, democracy is all right, but what I want is a job." When you hear that point of view expressed, democracy is in danger. If they have a choice they will choose the job. I wish they would choose-democracy, but after all they must live.
I have risen this afternoon because I want to put on record, not what Tom Jones told the hon. member for Renfrew North on the-train going west, or what some other gossip told him in Vancouver, but what the national employment commission said regarding this transient problem. I heard no protest from the minister in any shape or form. I say that type of statement regarding young men who honestly want work and are unable to get it is the type of thing which will lead to what hon. members to my left want and what I do not want, a complete upset of the system under which we are living.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Then I shall simply say they may not want to upset it but they want to turn it over. I am not particular as to the language; if the language hurts my hon. friend I will change it. But so far as I can see, they want-some of them-to take the bottom and put it on the top. I believe that the system under which we are living, the capitalistic system, the democratic system, is the best system, a system worthy of preservation, and I want to preserve it; but one of the surest ways to upset and destroy that system is to take the attitude that these boys wandering around in all sections of the country hungrily looking for work are nothing but bums, lazy men who do not want to find something to do. I am convinced that ninety per cent-I will not go higher than that-of the people out of employment today want work and nothing else.
Recently I was in my own city of Fort William. We have there a relief officer named Frank Blaine who has been in ch&ige of relief in that city for twenty-five or thirty years, one of the best relief officers I have ever known, a man who originally had the reputation of being a little difficult for the poor to deal with, but because of that I quote him all the more confidently; for it shows he
is not inclined to go to extremes in his viewpoint. Frank Blaine said in reply to a question of mine that ninety per cent of those on relief in the city of Fort William and elsewhere want work, and he has looked into the question very thoroughly. I was surprised, because frankly I had not thought that so large a percentage did want work. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) a few minutes ago quoted a letter he received from some young man. I suppose I have had hundreds of such letters; as a minister when we were in power I had many, and I have had hundreds recently of the same type. Recently I had a most pathetic letter from a mother; I think most hon. members receive such letters. I could name a man in this building at this moment, one who is working in a humble position and receiving about $100 a month, but he is living on it. One day I saw this man looking very much depressed and unhappy-this was when we were in power-and asked what was wrong, because he happened to be one of the civil servants with whom I came in contact quite frequently. He said he had a boy of twenty-three who could not get a job, who had never earned a dollar in his life. I asked where the boy was and he told me that he was in one of the labour camps, but that he wanted some work to do. He said, "I am afraid of his whole character being ruined because he cannot get any work to do." So in my office I gave instructions that the next time we were putting on a few labourers over here at the canal, as we did from time to time, this boy should be given a chance. That was done; he was given a pick and shovel job. Never in my 'life have I seen anyone more overjoyed than that father and that son when the boy came home after his first day of pick and shovel work.
Does that suggest that these boys do not want work? I quite agree with the hon. member for Macleod that you cannot argue a whole case from one instance; but you can argue a whole case from your knowledge of humanity; you can argue your case when you receive hundreds of letters from boys all over this country who ask for nothing but a job, who plead for the chance to earn a decent living. You can believe them in the great majority of cases; otherwise why would they bother to write letters? I also admit that many of them, because they cannot get jobs, are becoming demoralized; their whole character is becoming warped and twisted. That strikes me with particular force because I sat over on the government benches in 1932, 1933 and 1934. Many of my hon. friends opposite

were here at that time. The Minister of Labour was not in the house then, but well do I remember the abuse that was heaped upon us by the then opposition, the present government, despite the fact that we were going through a terrific world depression, because we did not cure the condition. Well *do I remember rising in my place-I think it was during the budget debate-and pointing out to the present right hon. Prime Minister, who was then leader of the opposition, that he and his party did not seem to realize the fact that we were going through a world depression. Now, however, when conditions are not half so bad as they were in 1933, we hear the Minister of Labour appeal to hon. members to put up with the failure of the government to find a cure for this condition, on the ground that it is a world condition. That is the same cry we put up. It will be remembered that in 1933 there were some thirty million unemployed in the industrial countries throughout the world. In the neighbouring country to the south there were some twelve to thirteen million unemployed. I do not know that the situation there is very much better now, but here we have the Minister of Labour making the statement that this government has done so much for unemployment. I will admit that it has attempted a few things, yet we find that at the present time, according to the bureau of statistics, there are some 491,000 unemployed in Canada.
I mentioned this matter during my speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne; I said the statistics put out by the Department of Labour were unfair and were not frank. I do not say they are untrue; I presume they are true as far as they go, but they present only half the truth. For example, in the last release dated April 8 the Minister of Labour says that the dominion total of unemployed but fully employable persons on aid in February of this year was
190,000.	I have before me the figures from the bureau of statistics, which show that in February there were 476,000 unemployed and in March, 491,000. That is their estimate, it is true; it is not an absolutely accurate figure, but these figures never can be absolutely accurate. I repeat what I said previously, however, that when the Minister of Labour gives out that figure of 190,000 on aid, probably that is the truth; I am not quarreling with it, but it does not present a true picture. According to the figures of the bureau of statistics there are another 300,000 who are not on aid but who are unemployed just the same. I admit that in the winter time in Canada there are always more unemployed.

When we were in power I sometimes tried to find out what would be the normal layoff during the winter season in this country, and I was told that it would be anywhere from 150,000 to 200,000. I imagine some such figure would be reasonably accurate, and the minister nods his head. If that is correct this figure of 491,000 is 300,000 or more in excess of what we might call normal.

I do not want to be unfairly critical of my hon. friends to my left, but too often they assume a sort of super-righteous attitude. They seem to think they alone have the vision to see the needs of our country, that they alone know the needs of youth. I want to say to them, as the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) pointed out, that away back in 1930 our party made a promise to cure unemployment. We did not succeed; after that promise was made we went through the worst depression the world has ever seen, without exception. Ever since then our party has endeavoured to help clean up this mess, because it is a mess. At our party convention nearly a year ago I said one of the first things I would do if I were to become leader of a government would be to appoint a ministry of youth. That would rather indicate that we know something about this problem. I believe all the members of this house would like to see this problem solved, but the fact is that the government has utterly failed to bring about that end. I will stick to the point as I see fit. The hon. gentleman who just interrupted me, who is one of the loudest speakers of all in regard to printing money, said in the house the other day that he would advocate the printing of about $600,000,000 more in bills. If that is not almost an unlimited amount of money then I do not know what it is. The hon. member nods his head in acceptance; I do not know why he interrupted me.	I rather enjoy the hon.
member's speeches; I do not know why he finds it so difficult to listen to mine. I may not be as artistic as he is, but I am doing my best.
The trouble is the failure of the government to recognize the condition and to take steps to correct it. I do not suggest for a moment that the government do not wish to end this problem, but certainly to my mind they have failed miserably to do so. In the first place they failed to carry out the suggestions that were made by the Purvis commission. I put them on record in my speech on the address, and I believe I have the twelve suggestions under my hand. These are the recommendations of the Purvis commission, made in its report to the government, about a year ago. I will read these recommendations, because they are brief. They recommended:
1.	A great national cooperative effort to end unemployment.
Nothing done about it that I know of.
2.	Employment services to be national.
The same remark applies there.
3.	Commission to be administrative, not just advisory.
Well, the commission has gone out of existence altogether.
4.	A proper registry of unemployed and their classification.
Nothing done.
5.	Local communities to help in the work through local committees.
Nothing done.
6.	Wiping out dole, which was to be replaced by rehabilitation measures.
I do not know of anything done there.
7.	Slum clearance.
Nothing done.
8.	The national body to be succeeded by a small administrative committee to be helped by an interdepartmental committee to prevent overlapping.
Nothing done.
9.	Financial provision for and administration of unemployment aid should be the responsibility of the dominion government.
That is not done.
Three I have left to the last, and they are partly done at any rate. They are apprenticeship and learnership, youth training, and housing plans. They are partly done. And recently, if I understood correctly from press reports, the Minister of Labour suggested that the government was going to spend a million dollars on forestry. That would be another project, although I do not know that it was recommended by the commission. It is not in my list, but I note it from a press report.
There is the list of twelve recommendations by the Purvis commission. Three of them are partly carried out. That was the condition, despite the fact that the Prime Minister after the last election-not before, but after the last election when he did not need to make promises, because he had already caught the street-car so to speak; he did not need to try to catch it because he had caught it and had caught it well, as far as that goes- made this promise, part of which I shall quote:
In the new era which dawns to-day-
And this is the evening after the election.
-the struggle for the rights of the people will, in the realm of economic liberty and security, be carried on as never before. Poverty and adversity, want and misery are the enemies which Liberalism will seek to banish from our land.
Then he went on further:
We take up at once, as our supreme task, the endeavour to end poverty in the midst of plenty; starvation and unnecessary suffering in a land of abundance; discontent and distress in a country more blessed by Providence than any other on the face of the globe, and to gain for individual lives, and for the nation as a whole, that "health and peace and sweet content" which is the rightful heritage of all.
He did not need to make all these promises. As I said, he had won the election. The election was over and the right hon. gentleman was elected. I have not any doubt he made the statement in all sincerity, but he has done nothing, or practically nothing, to carry it out. The attempts of his Minister of Labour have been almost wholly a failure. Therefore I repeat that the government is at

least partly and, I think, a great deal, to blame for the fact that we have to-day among our young men demoralization which should and could be largely eliminated, if those young men were given a chance to earn their living, as most of them want to do. Many of them have lost ambition, and the situation is getting worse. The demoralization and the loss of ambition get worse as we go on. Their morale has gone.
On other occasions I have said in the house and also elsewhere that to my mind much of the crime of youth is to-day caused by the fact that the young men are hopeless, despairing, and they start out and get into trouble which otherwise they would escape. We know that they are desperate and want to get positions. In many instances they go to gaol because they cannot get something to do.
It is in my opinion a national calamity that
we have not done more than we have to cure this condition, a condition which certainly, unless we succeed in curing it, will wreck the whole economic system under which we live. On many different occasions, out on the hustings, I have taken that attitude. I have spoken at public meetings about fears along the same lines as I am now stating. I believe the bringing together of the best brains in this country, all classes-

Speaking seriously, I believe we must have a pooling of the best brains in this country. I do not mind saying that on one occasion when we were in power I suggested to my then leader that we call in, to Ottawa, the outstanding men in business, in labour, the outstanding clergy, and the leading men in various other groups, and ask them to pool their ability in an endeavour to give us a solution of the problem. I am as much convinced of this as I am of anything. I feel convinced that those men who take that reactionary attitude, which was taken this afternoon particularly by the hon. member for Wellington North, and one or two others, that nothing can be done-and

the rumour is passed around, incidentally, that the Prime Minister-and I do not wish to misquote him-said the other day to his followers that there was no cure for the problem. He is quite right to correct the statement if it is wrong.

I will accept the statement of the Minister of Finance. However, I thought it might have been worth correcting, before my having misquoted it in the house- since the Minister of Finance takes the attitude that I am misquoting it.
If we do not cure this condition we shall have the collapse of our system. I repeat what I was saying, that I do not agree with those people who take the attitude that nothing can be done, or that young men can just get out and earn their living, as they have done in the past, and that opportunities are just as good as they were in the past. Those people who take that attitude are endangering our system. They lack vision. It was the same type of people who in other days and in other countries assumed the attitude that nothing could be done, and they and their countries paid for it.
I want to preserve the present system. I do not want to see it completely upset. I believe in what we call the capitalist system, or what is sometimes called the profit or reward system. But I believe that under it we can work out a cure for this condition, and that \ye must work out that cure if we are going to continue to preserve the system in which we believe.
That is my feeling, and that is why I am to-day expressing what I have expressed many times before, namely that I consider the greatest problems in our country are, on the one hand unemployment, and on the other the lack of opportunity for youth. We must correct those conditions if we are going to bring about a proper stabilization of the system in which most of us do believe.

speechtext:
I have in my hand a copy of the report of the director of the international labour conference at Geneva in 1937.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
I am not particularly impressed with the director of the international labour conference, but he cannot be accused of being a social crediter. He says this:
If the depression has shown one thing more clearly than anything else it is that economic prosperity and social security depend more on monetary policy than on any other single factor.
If we are to believe many hon. members who have spoken this afternoon our troubles are on account of the fact that a large percentage of the Canadian people are too lazy to work. They were referring to the unemployed. Well, I have always noticed that those who delight to sneer at the poor are always the ones who are so willing to lick the boots of the rich. I should like to repeat something I said in this chamber before. When a rich man gets out of bed, he is considered to be a hard working citizen, but when a poor man gets into bed, he is considered to be a lazy bum.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) has said that we in this corner wish to destroy what is known as the capitalist system. That is the exact opposite to the truth. We want to preserve the capitalist system, but we do want to destroy what is known as finance capitalism because that is the evil which is wrecking our civilization. It is our system of finance that is wrong. That is the greatest racket the world has ever known, and unless it is destroyed, it will ruin the civilization we know to-day. We are proposing a very simple thing, that is, that the state should see to it that the capitalist system is supplied with enough purchasing power to the end that we may be able to consume what we produce. Whenever we suggest that, we are accused of wanting to print unlimited money, of wanting to turn on the printing presses, but that is not the idea.
The other night I suggested something that I have suggested on several occasions, that we should and could pension off all people over the age of sixty years. The last time this motion was before the house the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) told us what it would cost. I never can remember figures, but I know the cost was many millions of dollars. But that really does not convey any meaning to us. We appreciate the difference between money and wealth. Just what would it cost? Suppose this house were to decide that the age limit for old age pensions should be lowered from seventy to sixty years, that would cost
815,000,000.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Just exactly what does that mean? It means that it will cost the people of Canada the work necessary to buy that
820,000,000. That is the way I look at it. Of course, before that was done this government would have to have the consent of the people of Canada, but if it were decided that the age limit should be reduced to sixty years the cost would be exactly the amount of work necessary to make that 820,000,000 of real wealth. If the Minister of Finance could say that everyone under the age of seventy years was working, that we had a certain standard of living, that the proposal to lower the age limit to sixty years would cost this country the wealth which is produced by everyone between the ages of sixty and seventy years, then that is what it would cost this country to lower the age limit for old age pensions. But that is not the position at all.
I believe there are over a million people on relief and half a million men with nothing to do. All that would happen would be that a certain number of older people would be relieved from work which they are too old to perform, and a chance would be given to a corresponding number of younger people who are looking for work. As a matter of fact, it would not cost the country a cent. That money would have to be bought or honoured, if you like, by the goods and services of the people of Canada. Is that not exactly what the people are clamouring to do? Are there not hundreds of thousands of men clamouring for work? Does not practically every hon. member of this committee say that what we have to do is to provide work? What is the objection to issuing money and then asking the people of Canada to honour it with their work?
I can remember when I started to farm years ago that we had no provincial government and therefore we had no local taxes. There was no trouble in raying our road taxes because we were allowed to work them out. All w-e had to do was to take our teams and work so many days on the road and our taxes were paid. There was no difficulty. But after a time the system of taxation became more complicated and there were more councillors who were making a living out of being councillors. They wanted more cash and so we had to pay more taxes in cash and less with work. The consequence was that our tax deficits mounted. In my riding are pioneer districts in which many men are only scratching out a living on small clearings which they have made in the bush, yet in some of the local improvement districts the taxes are behind to the extent of 8250,000. That is a ridiculous sum because it can never
2916	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
be paid in cash. Many of these farmers tell me that they do not handle more than five or six dollars in cash during the whole season. The roads in these municipalities had ceased to exist. The farmers could not find the cash with which to pay their taxes and they had not been allowed to work out their taxes. The Alberta government has introduced a system whereby these farmers can work out their back taxes. I understand they work, say three days; the work of two days is applied to the payment of back taxes, and they are given a tax remission slip to cover payment for the work of the third day, which slip can be exchanged for goods at the store. This offers an example of what a little cash can accomplish.
To say that our financial system liquidates itself is simply not the truth. If hon. members will read the report of the committee on banking and finance of the United States congress they will see that every member of that committee agrees with what we in this corner have said. While they may not agree with the exact method to be adopted, they do agree with us when we say that industry is unable to distribute sufficient purchasing power to permit the. consumption of what it makes. This statement is no longer generally doubted. Apparently this chamber is one of the few places where it is doubted. I do not want to prolong this debate, but I do want to suggest: instead of putting the blame on the unfortunate victims of this depression, why not for a change indulge in a little criticism of those who were responsible for it? There should be more criticism of the men who were responsible for the financial policies which brought about this depression-the victims of the depression are blameless.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE USE OF THE WORD "BUTTER" TO DESIGNATE CERTAIN PRODUCTS

speechtext:
Mr. J. H. LECLERC (Shefford) moved the second reading of Bill No. 44, to amend the Dairy Industry Act.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, as this is the first
occasion on which I address the house in the English language, I crave the kind indulgence of my English-speaking colleagues. Because of the general interest attaching to-this bill to amend the Dairy Industry Act, the second reading of which I now have the honour to move, I desire to explain its object in a language which all will understand.
Most hon. members undoubtedly realize that among the numerous problems which our governments are called upon to solve, those relating to agriculture stand paramount. I do not delude myself to the point of believing that this bill will remove all the difficulties under which the dairy industry is labouring, but I think it will do much tp prevent the encroachments of the numerous substitutes sold under false representations contrary to the spirit of the Dairy Industry Act, which defines butter as being "the food product commonly known as butter which is manufactured exclusively from milk or cream or both, with or without the addition of colouring matter, common salt, or other harmless preservatives."
We have a law to protect maple sugar and maple syrup in their natural state; we have stringent enactments designed to protect the trade marks of many private brands of foodstuffs. I therefore submit that, when we take such action in matters of limited interest, we should in all justice take steps to remove the unfair competition to which butter, which is of general interest and needs still greater protection, is at present subjected from numerous substitutes such as peanut butter, cocoa butter, chocolate butter, caramel butter, orange butter, strawberry butter, honey butter, sugar butter and so on.
In order to prove to the house the number of substitutes sold under the name of butter I have brought into the chamber a few samples of these substitutes. I have a jar of peanut butter, and there are half a dozen brands of sugar butter, which is nothing but ordinary sugar melted, some water together with a certain quantity of flavouring matter having been added. I have here a 32-ounce package of soft sugar which sells for twenty-five cents, while the untreated sugar is sold at 5 cents a pound. I have here some chocolate butter which sells at a higher price than real butter. I have several samples of honey butter and chocolate butter.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE USE OF THE WORD "BUTTER" TO DESIGNATE CERTAIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Has the hon. member
any maple sugar?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE USE OF THE WORD "BUTTER" TO DESIGNATE CERTAIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
No, but I suggest that if the substitutes were made of maple sugar they would not be so bad. As a matter of fact they are made of white sugar, and we have in consequence a poor substitute or no substitute at all for butter.
Dairy Industry Act

The object of this measure is not only to preserve the reputation of the product but also to increase the consumption thereof. In fact I believe that we have reached the point where the displacing of Canadian butter by an infinity of substitutes, mostly of foreign origin, should not be tolerated. Canada's imports and consumption of these products in 1936 amounted to the impressive figure of some 15,000,000 pounds. While I do not claim that this great quantity of substitutes will be entirely replaced by butter, I think it is logical to believe that these products, sold under false pretences, do replace butter without having anything like its food value, no matter at what price they are sold. The object of my amendment is not to prevent the sale of these foreign products; it will still be permitted to offer them on the basis of their respective merits. I trust that all hon. members, having in mind the interests of agriculture, especially of dairy farming, will support this amendment, which will to a certain extent, I hope, prevent foreign products of questionable food value from displacing Canadian butter, which is the basic industry of the majority of Canadian farmers.
The present situation of the farmers of Canada is, I believe, well known to all hon. members representing rural constituencies. Having had the privilege of growing up on a farm and having been in the dairy business all my life, I may be better informed than many others respecting the true situation of this industry whose prosperity I ardently desire to promote, so that it may afford a decent living to those for whom it is the main source of income.
There is no need for me to point out again, Mr. Speaker, the difficulties with which the dairy farmers are faced. I set forth their legitimate grievances on June 22 last, and I do not think the situation has changed very much since that time. Allow me to repeat, however, that the dairy industry has never afforded more than a modest existence to the farmer, inasmuch as when there is a surplus of production, as at present, it has to be sold on the British market in competition with the products of countries better organized and far more favoured by nature to produce butter at a lower cost than that at which we can produce it. Since it is impossible for us to compete with such countries on an economic basis, we should seek to limit our production of butter to the actual needs of our population and to increase its consumption. Such is the object of this amendment, prompted entirely by my desire to render a service to the dairy industry, that most important branch of agriculture which fills such a great place in the economic life of Canada.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE USE OF THE WORD "BUTTER" TO DESIGNATE CERTAIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I appreciate highly the aim of the hon. member who introduced this bill. I quite agree with him that the dairy industry faces a rather serious situation, one which has been thrust upon us because science and invention have supplanted many of the things which we used in former days, and we have had to turn to dairying to provide a market in lieu of many commodities which once were grown at a profit on the farm. Before the advent of the automobile not only had we a market for the horses to which we fed our hay and oats, but when we sold the horses we were also able to sell feed to maintain them in the cities. Now it is necessary for us to take the products of our fields and turn them into revenue on the farms, and to do that we have increased our output of dairy products.
As the hon. member pointed out, one of the great difficulties we are facing to-day is the competition from various substitutes for butter. Barnum was not so far wrong when he said that people liked to be fooled. The same statement is still applicable, because to-day people do not always spend their money wisely in the purchase of foods. When they buy substitutes for a good wholesome product like butter they do not in fact obtain very much value for their money. After all, the quality of a food product has a great bearing upon its value and the results you get from your expenditure.
I am inclined to the view that it might be a good idea to insist upon analyses of various products which come into competition with our basic foodstuffs and have the results registered. Under present conditions, we do not treat human beings with as much consideration as we give to the live stock on our farms, because when we buy bran, oil cake and other foods for our cattle and horses, the law requires that such commodities shall contain certain percentages of proteins, fats and carbohydrates. Yet human beings can buy any product for their own consumption without regard to its food value. It seems to me that if the hon. member had included in his bill a provision of the kind I have mentioned he would have made an important contribution toward educating the public in getting proper value for their money. Many object to paying twenty-five cents for five or six pounds of oatmeal, yet people will pay about $6 for a bushel of corn in the form of com flakes. The amount of money expended and the food value received are not at all comparable. It might do something to solve the problem of unemployment if society were furnished with proper food at an economic price. Much is said about the fact that the

Dairy Industry Act
great necessities of humanity are food, clothing and shelter, yet when we are prepared to pay about $6 a bushel for com in the form of corn flakes it makes one wonder whether we are attacking this problem seriously, seeing we have within our own control methods of dealing with it. If these commercial products were required to bear a statement showing their actual food values, under penalty of being debarred from the market, it would go a long way toward reducing the competition which producers of good creamery butter now have to meet.
In this day and generation science seems to be doing everything possible to find substitutes for the real thing. Doctors recommend the use of vitamins, and much stress is laid on the importance of a balanced ration, but if we continue to develop these synthetic substances it may be wondered just what the human race will come to in a few years. I hold in my hand a report on the United States butter industry, and I note that research organizations in that country have developed a new product from whey, which as hon. members know is a by-product of the manufacture of cheese. The name of this product is Polymethylacrylate, and there is no doubt that it can be produced. It is a water white semi-transparent material, closely related to the glass used in highway reflectors. It is softer and more flexible than organic glass, but very tough and lasting. I mention that to show that many articles may be made out of dairy products; the resources of science and invention in this direction are not exhausted. By this means new uses may be found for some of our dairy products. I am led to believe that the casein of milk can be used in many articles produced as substitutes for rubber. The possibilities along this line are comparable with those of the soya bean. I am told that about a hundred different articles can be made from the soya bean. We would be within our rights if in view of the serious situation which we are now facing, we made an effort to increase the production of substitutes manufactured from dairy products.
I believe it would be money well spent if the Department of Agriculture would make some effort, by means of advertising over the radio and in the newspapers, to show the food value of butter as compared with that of other products. After all, if a nation is to be strong it is necessary that it should have good food. A good many products are put on the market simply to sell, with no food value in them at all. I often wonder at the taste we have developed for soft drinks and mineral waters of various kinds. There is absolutely no food value in these beverages, and I sometimes think if they were called drugs, which 71492-184
after all they are, and banned as beverages, we might substitute for them something that would have actual food value. I believe science has developed a process by which apple cider now can be kept without losing its sweetness, and it would be much better if those soft drink bottles were filled with good apple cider or even grape juice. Then the people would get some food value; I believe their health would be the better for it, and industry would be helped. I quite understand that people have a right to buy what they like, but I think we would be quite within our rights if we banned anything that might be detrimental to the physical well-being of our people. T remember that several years ago an embargo was placed upon the use of oleomargarine, just because it was not considered a good food for humanity. We as Canadian citizens felt that if we were to maintain a strong, virile and intelligent people it was necessary to have good food, and when oleomargarine was analyzed it was found that on the basis of food value it was much more expensive than butter.
I believe that is the angle from which we should approach this sort of legislation; that is, on the basis of actual food value. I believe it is possible that we would materially improve the health of our nation if we confined ourselves to those products which contain high food values, so I am glad to recommend the use of butter in place of some of these substitutes. I think on that ground there is a great deal of justification for a movement to eliminate substitutes, which endeavour to fool the people into believing they are getting more value than actually is the case.
Once more I am going to suggest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that money invested in an endeavour, by means of radio and newspaper advertising, to increase the demand for good, wholesome farm products would be money well spent. It might be pointed out to the housewives that every cent spent on good wholesome food is a good investment. I have great confidence in the intelligence of the Canadian people, and I believe they would respond to an advertisement of this kind. At the present time there is quite a controversy in regard to the substitution of vegetable oils for dairy products, mainly for use in baking. In spite of the fact that vegetable shortening is less expensive than lard, I do not believe it is as good an investment. After all, it should be cheaper, because it has not the same food value. I sometimes think the Minister of Agriculture should insist that all these articles be labeled to show their food value; I think at this time we have a right to insist on that.

Dairy Industry Act

I have before me an example of what advertising has done in connection with fish, and I think we must give a great deal of credit to our friends from the maritimes and British Columbia for the way in which they have advertised their products. I have before me a nice advertisement which appeared in the National Home Monthly. Naturally, after coming across an advertisement like this in a magazine, at the first opportunity a good housewife would tell her husband to bring home some fish for supper, and I have no doubt that advertisements of this kind have had a tendency to stimulate the demand for fish. I believe our friends in Prince Edward Island are doing a very good job of advertising Prince Edward Island potatoes. I know that in the section of the country in which I live we buy many, many carloads of potatoes from that province. I do not know whether they are any better potatoes than we could grow ourselves, but they have us thinking they are better, and we keep buying them year after year. I have come to the conclusion that happiness is a state of mind; that it is not what people have in their pockets or what they have in their cellars that makes them happy, but the state of their minds.
Perhaps this has no bearing on the question, . but I believe that if you advertise a product as being good it is necessary that you make a good product. So far as butter is concerned,
I believe Manitoba has won more prizes than any other province. I have in my hand a smart bulletin issued by that province which states that Manitoba won 57-6 per cent of all prizes awarded for creamery butter at the ten largest fairs held in Canada during 1938. So I am inclined to take the view that I would gladly recommend to the Minister of Agriculture such an advertising campaign, which I believe would have a tendency to relieve the surplus that exists to-day. At the same time I would urge him to give consideration to some measure which would require these products to indicate their food value.
I have every reason to believe that the intelligent housewife will take cognizance of that, and that she will endeavour to secure the very best for her money.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE USE OF THE WORD "BUTTER" TO DESIGNATE CERTAIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to support the measure presented by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Leclerc) to amend the Dairy Industry Act, the purpose of the bill being to prevent the use, to the detriment of butter producers and consumers, of the word " butter," for the sale of products which are not butter, as defined in our Dairy Industry Act.

It would seem to me that such a measure would be conducive to salutary effects on the dairy industry at all times. But even more do we find good reasons for the introduction of the bill to-day, when the dairy industry is such that all possible means must be used to come to its assistance. Especially is this true of that branch of dairying connected with butter production.
On account of exceptionally good pasturing conditions last summer and, I might add, on account also of speculation in butter, this country finds itself with such a surplus of butter that the prospects for the coming year are none too reassuring to those engaged in that branch of dairying. If we do not want to see prices which will be almost suicidal to Canadian butter producers, some action must be taken.
As is well known to all hon. members well versed in the matter, 95 per cent of our butter production is consumed locally and, roughly speaking, 5 per cent is exported. But it is this excess of exportable production which, generally speaking, fixes the price on our home markets. It would appear to me that not only could this excess of 5 per cent of our consumption be taken care of, but the efforts of all concerned in the industry should be directed toward taking care of this 5 per cent over-production in such a way that it should not control the price of the other 95 per cent produced.
As much as possible this excess production should foe diverted to other channels. For example, it could be made into cheese. Then, again there could foe a greater consumption of natural milk, or other dairy products. Also, educational campaigns both in this country and abroad should enhance and make better known our dairy products, especially our cheese, which has no equal throughout the entire world.
Again, in our trade treaties with other countries the greatest anxiety should be shown in finding favourable outlets for our excess butter production. Incidentally, I might state that I do not view with great satisfaction the information contained in a recent bulletin showing imports of butter into the United Kingdom, where it was revealed that of a total import necessity of 1,000,000,000 pounds, empire countries, not including Canada, supplied about 535,000,000 pounds, foreign countries supplied a total of 527,000,000 pounds, while Canada supplied only three and one-third million pounds. It would seem to me that surely ways and means should be devised in order that it might be possible to have more

Dairy Industry Act
Canadian butter shipped to the United Kingdom market especially, to replace that coming into England from foreign countries.
The hon. member for Shefford has informed the house that last year alone some 15,000,000 pounds of butter preparations, labeled "butter" but not in fact being butter in the sense accepted by the Dairy Industry Act, were imported into Canada for consumption. Added to this amount must also be taken into consideration the number of pounds of these same preparations which were made in Canada and sold as substitutes for butter.
As I understand it, it is not the purpose of the bill to bring about a condition whereby none of these preparations will continue to be placed on the market for consumption. The bill would make provision whereby it would no longer be possible to place products labeled "butter" on the market. It is safe to assume, therefore, that should this restriction respecting the use of the word "butter" be applied to the products in question, less of those products would be sold to replace butter, and the dairy industry would surely benefit by selling more butter for local consumption than it has sold in the past. I believe the protection offered by the bill is a step in the right direction, and I am convinced that the dairy industry is ready to support the measure.
If all who are interested in the success of the dairy industiy are to strive to do their utmost to have the products of that industry obtain a wider market and secure more favourable prices, surely by corollary should we likewise exert all possible care in connection with any possible substitutes for dairy products. That is the object of the bill, and with it I am heartily in accord.

Mr. Speaker, I think this bill should have been designated, "The Eastern Townships Bill." Hon. members from the eastern townships have not spoken in the house very often, which may be taken as an evidence that they are perfectly satisfied and in accord with everything that has been done. I wish, however, to lend my support to the bill presented by my colleague, the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Leclerc), and I believe it should be passed. I do not think there is any member of the house who is not of the same mind.
Hon. members are aware of the condition in which the dairy industry of Canada finds itself to-day. We know about the surplus of butter on hand. In view of the array of exhibits placed before the house by the hon. member who introduced the measure, I think it will be readily realized that the butter producers are up against heavy competition. The 71492-184}
hon. member might have added two more to his list, namely maple butter and cocoa butter. It is only a short time ago when the domestic shortening producers were placing on their labels the words, "Just as good as butter."
So I say it is about time we were giving the butter industry a little protection. One point I would make is that any assistance extended to the dairy industry is assistance given to the small producer. As a result of the foresight of provincial governments in 1934, when dairy commissions were appointed, large producers of fluid milk for the fluid milk market were taken care of. The only producer to-day who is looking for assistance is the small producer who is compelled to go to the butter factory. When I refer to the large producer I am of course referring to the man who is maintaining a large herd of dairy cattle. Invariably that man is delivering his product to the fluid milk market, and in that respect he is fortunate.
I know of some hon. members who are enjoying that privilege. For instance, in the province of Quebec the price of three and a half per cent milk to-day varies from 82 to $2.25 per 100 pounds. All producers are supplying milk averaging over three and a half per cent. I may say that the milk delivered in Montreal to-day, the largest milk market in the dominion, where more than 850,000 pounds of milk are consumed daily, in addition to ice-cream and special milk drinks, averages 3-8 per cent butter fat. The producer enjoys also a bonus of three cents for every tenth of a point over the three and a half per cent. Contrast that condition with the condition which faces the dairy farmer who is compelled to sell his cream to the butter factory for eighty cents per 100 pounds and has only the skim-milk left. This government should not do what has been done in many instances, namely, help the man who does not need assistance; this government should be trying to help the small dairy farmer who really is in distress.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE USE OF THE WORD "BUTTER" TO DESIGNATE CERTAIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Leclerc) upon bringing this matter to the attention of the house. If there is any class in Canada to-day deserving of consideration, it is the dairy farmer. There is no class of farmer who suffers more to-day than the dairy farmer who is producing milk and sending it to the butter factory or manufacturing it into butter himself. There are a number of reasons for this condition, but I shall not deal with all of them to-night. The question before
Dairy Industry Act

the house at this time is a bill to amend the Dairy Industry Act. The one section of this bill reads:
Section 5 of the Dairy Industry Act, chapter forty-five of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, is amended by adding immediately after paragraph (e) thereof, the following paragraph :
" (f) use the word 'butter' to describe, label, advertise, sell or offer for sale, a product different from the product defined in paragraph (a) of section two of this act."
Section 5 of the act reads:
No person shall
(a)	manufacture, import into Canada, or offer, sell or have in his possession for sale, any oleomargarine, margarine, butterine, or other substitutes for butter, manufactured wholly or in part from any fat other than that of milk or cream;
(b)	mix or incorporate with butter, by any process of heating, soaking, reehurning, reworking, or otherwise, any cream, milk, skim milk, buttermilk or water to cause such butter when so treated to contain over sixteen percentum of water or less than eighty percentum of milk fat.
Paragraph (e) reads:
(e) have upon premises occupied by him where any dairy produce is treated, manipulated, manufactured, or reworked, any substance that might be used for the adulteration of any such product and the presence upon any such premises of any fat or oil capable of being used for such adulteration shall be prima facie proof of intent so to use it.
I have before me samples of seven different products each of which is labeled "butter." The first is called Golden Bar Chocolate- Honey Butter, and it sells for ten cents for four ounces. I have here another called Meadow Sweet Sugar Butter, which is composed of caramel, coconut and chocolate. This sells for thirteen cents a pound, but in its original state, apart from the flavouring, it would cost about four cents a pound. We are not complaining about a manufacturer selling such products, if he can sell them, or the consumer buying them, if he wants them; what we are complaining about is the fact that articles of this type are termed "butter." Surely the dairy cow should have a monopoly of the use of the word "butter."

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE USE OF THE WORD "BUTTER" TO DESIGNATE CERTAIN PRODUCTS
speechtext: What about butternuts?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE USE OF THE WORD "BUTTER" TO DESIGNATE CERTAIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I have here another type of butter made of sugar, which sells at twenty-five cents for less than two pounds. The sugar from which it is made would cost about five cents a pound, yet the manufacturer is permitted to sell this under the name of butter. I submit again that the dairy cow should have complete monopoly of the use of the word "butter." If we go back as far as history, records we find that the people knew what

butter was. We are told about butter in the book of Proverbs. This is something that is contained in the book of Proverbs:
Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter.
Another objection to permitting these substitutes to be sold as butter is the fact that very often the manufacturers advertise them as being equal to butter in food value. At one time that was more or less generally believed, but it has since been proven that such is not the case. Butter is composed mainly of milk fat. A considerable amount of water is present and, in addition, a small amount of casein and usually some salt. The proportion of each ingredient present in any sample depends upon the process of manufacture. The fat varies as a rule between 79 and 82 per cent in factory-made butter, while the water ranges from 12 to nearly 16 per cent. Under the national laws, butter in the United States having a water content above 16 per cent must pay a tax of ten cents a pound as adulterated butter if it enters into interstate sommerce. The casein, or curd, furnishes about one per cent of the whole. The salt varies between 1-5 and 3-5 per cent, two per cent being a standard figure. There is a considerable demand in large cities for unsalted butter.
Butter has been prized as a food as far back as the beginning of written history. As a source of energy for the body, butter has about the same value as other fats, such, as coconut oil, lard and cottonseed oil. Those interested in the manufacture and sale of butter substitutes have made use of this fact by claiming that substitutes for butter made from animal and vegetable oils are equal to butter as human food. But scientific discoveries of recent years show that butter fat contains an exceedingly important substance known as a vitamin which is absent from or found in very minute quantities in vegetable oils and animal fats other than butter.
This is something of importance: Without this vitamin, which may likewise be obtained from milk, children and animals cannot grow. For this reason there is no real substitute for butter, and the farmer who sells his cream or butter and buys a substitute is risking the health and growth of his family, and especially the normal development of the children.
The house should seriously consider passing this measure. We are quite willing that the manufacturers of Golden Bar-Honey Butter, sugar butter, or peanut butter, should go on manufacturing their substitutes if they wish, but we contend that they ought not to be allowed to describe them by the name of 'butter."

Dairy Industry Act

But it is butter, made from butter fat, the product of a dairy cow, and I contend that the dairy cow was first in the field, and that her monopoly ought to be preserved, not be allowed to be infringed by people who would give us a mixture of white sugar and I do not know what, corn starch or anything they care to use, and call it butter. No animal in this or any other country deserves as much credit as the dairy cow. All over Canada farmers who farm on a small scale have been able to build up homes and provide a living for a family largely by means of a few good dairy cows; that has been the case all through the years. Now we have these manufacturers of substitutes-and the number is growing; we have, I think, eight-continually finding something new for which they try to take the name that ought to be kept exclusively for the product of the cow. As far back as history goes, "butter" meant the product of the cow, and the word ought to be restricted to that product. We do not need a patent if this law goes into effect.
An hon. member asked what these substitutes should be called. Lest the manufacturers should have trouble in finding a name for themselves, I suggest that they brand their products "substitute butter," so that when the housewife goes into a store for butter she will not be fooled into carrying away something else. I am inclined to think we have been backward in educating our people to the real value of dairy butter. I suppose there is no other product that contains as much food value in an equal space as a piece of good butter. With the regulations surrounding the manufacture of butter as we have them today it is a rare thing to find butter of poor quality in our restaurants or eating places. I should like to draw forcibly to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture this important anmedment to the Dairy Act, and I hope
that by this time next year our dairy men will be protected to the extent that the word "butter" may be reserved solely for the product of the dairy cow.

Hon. members opposite from the eastern townships support a policy of protection for butter and yet are opposed to any protection for manufactured goods. The hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) is strong for protection on butter for his own district but will deny any protection on manufactured goods for the rest of Canada. The Conservative party believe in the real doctrine of protection; they were the authors and founders of protection in this country. I am for a policy of protection, all for each and each for all. I believe that the right application of the doctrine of protection, brought up to date to meet modern conditions, would solve all the economic ills in all the provinces. I was ridiculed when I proposed in 1923 a national fuel policy of bonuses, subventions and subsidies for the coal of the maritime provinces, Alberta and Wales, so as to use an all-British coal supply. Sir Henry Thornton said that it was a lunch-counter system of freight rates. But I said that was better than sending $56,000,000 in wages to his friends the Pennsylvania coal barons. I told him, we are far better off with a lunch-counter system of freight rates protecting our coal industry than supporting the Pennsylvania coal barons. subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS-UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
At six o'clock when the committee rose I was reading a letter sent to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) from the young men of John Frank's house. In the earlier part of the letter they made a request. Then the letter continues:
Consequently in making this application for the privilege of doing useful, gainful work we wish to offer ourselves as a group to demonstrate how a small works camp would work out. Although there are a variety of works projects on which such a group as ours might be employed, the following suggestions may prove practical.
Remember, these young men wish to be employed as a group. They rehabilitated themselves with the help of public-spirited citizens of Toronto, and they have been doing admirable work with the aid of the Reverend. John Frank, a fine Christian gentleman. These are some of the projects:
(A)	Trans-Canada highwayconstruction work.
(B)	National parksdevelopment and clearing
roads
reforestation.
(C)	Flood control workon navigable waterways.
We have given much thought to this matter and believe that such an experimental camp would be better if planned as a straight works project. On this basis it would be necessary and logical that such personnel as engineer, government clerk, timekeeper, foreman, and powder man be appointed from outside our group. Such positions as straw bosses, blacksmith, carpenter, stable boss, and compressor man, however, could be filled capably from amongst our own numbers.
In our opinion, a fair wage scale for such an experimental camp would be 35 cents per hour minimum for labour, less nominal charges for housing, board and medical care.
We should like to emphasize that we consider this camp suggestion as a worthwhile experiment, a test case, and believe that the results obtained will provide much definite information of a kind which will aid in solving Canada's unemployment problem.
Our record as a group in John Frank's house is open to any inspection. We believe we have proven ourselves to be orderly, responsible citizens; but we do not wish to continue to live on charity. Our only request is for decent, honest work of value to our country and at wages on which we can live and find some hope for the future.
In making this application, may we respectfully ask your prompt consideration of it and an immediate reply? Our reason in asking this is that John Frank's house will close on April 1st.
Yours respectfully,
Single unemployed men of John Frank's House per S. Lyle,
House Committee.
These are the yaps, the spineless, pap-fed creatures, so called by the Liberal member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair), for which statement he was applauded by all hon. members on the Liberal benches. I wonder what the reply of the Minister of Labour was to these men. I do not know what it was, but the betting is that it was hedged round with constitutional difficulties and the kernel of that reply was, "Well, we won't help you."
The minister has lost one of the greatest opportunities any Minister of Labour ever had. Here is a group of young men, a crosssection of the country, who had rehabilitated themselves with the aid of public-spirited citizens. What an opportunity this was to see if that experiment could not continue to work, by giving these men a section of the trans-Canada highway to look after, or putting them on the reforestation of Canada's parks or some such program as that! I am sure this could have been done and had it cost the government anything, which is doubtful, the money would have been well spent.
What were these young men to do? Were they to go through the same old grind again, the same old wandering from pillar to post and finding themselves ultimately in the same old position that they occupied before? Were they the spineless creatures that they have been pictured to us? No. These boys are decent. Most of them left home, coming from all parts of Canada, because they could not bear to see the privation of those who were endeavouring to support them. I have met them, I have talked with them, and I know they are good Canadian citizens. I repeat, what were they going to do? They went farming. These so-called spineless boys got busy and enlisted the support of public-spirited citizens in Toronto; now they have a farm, and I see it reported in one of the daily newspapers that their funds now amount to $782. That is what these ninety men have done, and I say that the government has lost an opportunity to carry out an experiment that might have turned out to be very useful indeed.
There are between 50,000 and 100,000 of these men in Canada, and I am sure that if they were given the same treatment and had an opportunity to rehabilitate themselves they would be very soon taken off the relief payrolls. There are thousands of them between the ages of eighteen and twenty-five who have never had jobs.
One word about crime. All we have to do is to consult the police reports of hold-ups. One is astonished at the youth of those who are arrested as criminals, astonished at the age
(Mr. Deputy Speaker.]

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
at which they are sent to prison. This afternoon my leader (Mr. Manion) said that he thought this unemployment among these youths was responsible to a great extent for the crimes that are reported. I quote, as I quoted once before in this house, a dispatch from the Globe and Mail of January 20:
Mr. Neeland, deputy provincial secretary, in commenting on the jump in crime stated that, "the number of prison sentences in Ontario would reach a new high-higher than the previous record of 21,421 in 1930."
What a picture to have presented to us in Canada! Let us look at conditions in Toronto to-day. There are over 70,000 people on relief in that city. There are more people legitimately on relief in Toronto than ever before. If to-day we had the same policy of administration in Toronto with respect to relief as we had in 1934, there would be 130,000 or 140,000 people on relief-a terrible situation. There are 1,112,000 on relief in Canada,
491,000	workers unemployed and thousands of others on short time, and about one-third of the population of Canada are receiving less than 8450 a year.
When I go home every weekend, dozens of these people come to see me, people who cannot get work. Certainly they do not want relief, because when the average relief is $10 per capita per month, nobody wants to stay on relief. But they cannot get work. It gets a fellow down when he cannot do anything about the matter. The Liberal provincial member in my riding is just " run ragged " all the time. He so stated the other day in the provincial house. The situation is terrible. I receive dozens and dozens of letters from parents wanting to know why something cannot be done, why they cannot get jobs for their boys or their girls of seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty, twenty-three, twenty-four years of age who have never had any work. That is the situation in Toronto. Why does the government not get busy and put into effect some of the suggestions made by the employment commission? The minister says that the only opportunity for these young men is in agriculture. I do not agree. With the statistics before us of the products we consume in this country, surely we could see to it that a larger proportion of those products is made in Canada.
I have mentioned before that last year we imported agricultural implements of the value of around $19,000,000, and mining machinery to the extent of seven and a half million dollars; is it not possible for Canadians ta make some of this machinery? It seems to me that, following a proper survey by this government, they could see to it- that more
opportunities were provided for employment in industry. After all, the fanners can hardly make a living; as a general rule they do not want any more help; so industry seems to be almost the only alternative, although there are opportunities in forestry as well. The government are always disclaiming liability for unemployed employables, but if it is not their Obligation I do not know whose it is. Certainly the provincial governments have nothing to do with the provision of work in private industry, although they can provide some employment on public works projects. However, provincial governments have spent so much money on relief works that surely this government could take upon itself a program of reforestation or adopt some other of the suggestions which, for example, have been presented by the John Frank's house.
I noticed to-day an editorial in the Globe and Mail alluding to a million dollar forestry plan to employ some 4,000 young men. Why only 4,000 men; why not 40,000 in forestry if that number need work? Forestry and afforestation are useful and profitable; they will grow into money as time goes on and take up the slack in the meantime. Something must foe done. I am going to quote from a letter from Mr. W. F. Kirk, principal of the Jesse Ketchum school. He says:
The youth leaving school with high ideals for the future, finding himself in an indifferent society, becomes hostile to that society. We, to whom this country afforded such rare opportunity in our youth, cannot blame him for the loss of morale.
With the wonderful natural resources and oportunities we have in Canada, surely something could be done. The debt we are creating is far greater than any money debt; it represents the terrible liability of degraded youth; and when one remembers what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said after his election and sees what has happened in the last three and a half years, one ceases to wonder that Red agitators have such an easy time with some of our young men.

I should like to say to those hon. gentlemen that in my opinion some of the

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
statements which, were made this afternoon will do more harm across Canada than all the organizers who could be brought into this country. I doubt if anything would do more to undermine the morale of young men who are victims of an economic condition than to feel that those who sit in positions of responsibility in this house could use such libelous and scurrilous terms in referring to them.
I need hardly remind the committee that the attitude of some hon. gentlemen towards this class of people has changed from year to year. I have in mind the year 1935 when this same class of men

transients-were seeking to come to Ottawa to air their grievances. I remember that at that time. I followed Hansard very closely; I recall some of the crocodile tears which were shed by members of the then opposition, and that the hon. gentleman who is now Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) became eloquent 'and sentimental about these homeless lads These boys who had a just grievance in 1935 are dubbed in 1939 by the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) as having-a majority of them-a prison record, although he gave no statistics to substantiate his statement.

speechtext: That was not the statement at all. I think the hon. member was referring to some men who took part in the Vancouver riot last year.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS-UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Well, the hon. member can correct his own statement. I am sure that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) does not have to take a brief for the entire group across the way. If my statement is not accurate the hon. member is quite capable of correcting it. Those who had a just grievance in 1935 are now referred to as sabotageurs, as cutting hoses and as being unwilling to work. As the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) said, those charges of cutting hoses were entirely disproved.
The unemployed man in Canada to-day is on the horns of a dilemma. If he stays at home, assuming his parents are on relief, he can get relief but his prospects of getting a job are very small. If he leaves home in search of work, in a very short time he forfeits his residence qualification and ceases to be eligible for relief if he comes back home. Yes, I was going to say he is damned if he does and damned if he doesn't, but I did not know whether that remark was parliamentary. Either he must stay at home and accept relief without any prospect of a job, or he must go out to hunt a job and lose the right of any sustenance he might get through relief, because

he cannot come home again and live on the meagre relief allowance his parents are getting. That is the position of these men.
I have some case records relating not only to men in Canada but to some in the United States, where they are faced with the same problem. Scores of young men who have homes will not go back to those homes because, if they do, it means that the rest of the family must share the relief allowance with them. That is why I asked the minister this afternoon for an explanation of what seemed to be an unfair and misleading statement when he said that during the winter months there is no province or municipality in which provision is not made for unemployed men; later this afternoon the minister himself said that there were somewhat under 10,000 such young men not provided for. If the minister will clear our public gallery any afternoon he can fill it with young men from the city of Ottawa who are receiving no relief; they may be getting tickets at the mission, but no one has accepted direct responsibility to see that they are either properly cared for or have employment.	'
Now, when we ask the minister, what about these people?-his reply, at any rate this afternoon, is that agriculture is open to them, and at the same time he states that last year the employment service in the city of Ottawa placed 1,300 young men. Surely the minister must be cognizant of the fact that this would not begin to fill the need in Ottawa. I have here the report of the unemployment survey conducted by the Ottawa youth federation. The minister knows, probably better than I do, what was done here. They divided the city of Ottawa into, I think, forty-five districts and formed contacts with a number of families in each district. In all they covered 9,365 individuals, and what did they find? They found that the unemployed among these people, between the ages of sixteen and thirty and over thirty, numbered 938, or approximately ten per cent. That is a rough estimate, but here in the city of Ottawa, there is somewhere in the neighbourhood of ten per cent of these residents unemployed and capable of filling more than the 1,300 vacancies that may exist in connection with agricultural work. I know that in the parts of western Canada with which 1 am familiar, during the last two or three falls in areas where there have been crops, transients have poured in- because they heard of the crops and thought they might get work in the fields. What happened? In most instances the labour created by the crops could not absorb our local unemployed in the villages, towns and cities of western Canada, let alone provide
.vPRIL 18, 1939
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
work for the transients. There may have been the odd transient who obtained work, but in the main they could not get it.
I resent men rising in this house and saying that these people do not want to work. As yet I have not later figures from the minister; during this discussion I will ask for them, but he did give me the figures in regard to 1937-38. When the farm placement scheme opened in Saskatchewan in the fall of 1937 they received a little over 25,000 applications in a little more than thirty days, as the minister knows. Then they closed the books. Of those who applied, some 5.000, or roughly 20 per cent, were rejected; the rest went out and worked for $5 a month plus an extra 82.50 a month if they stayed throughout the entire winter. When anyone says these young people do not want to work they have only to look at these figures. Most of these people were on relief or had been on relief; yet, as I say, during the course of a month 25,000 of them signified their willingness to go on farms; as a matter of fact more signified their willingness to go out under this scheme than the government were prepared to put out. The minister suggests that agriculture is the only employment open to these young men.
