The hon. member is quite at liberty to make his speech after I am through, and he can show that it is not true.
I now turn to a statement made by the minister this afternoon. In a pettish way he suggested that all the members over here seemed to be able to think of was employment in terms of public work rather than private work. Of course that is not a fair statement. But the minister knows, just as every hon. member knows, that private employment has not been forthcoming; and when private employment is not forthcoming, the unemployed of this country have a right to think in terms of public employment. Of course I know the minister is definitely on record in that connection. I refer to his statement on February 17, 1936, appearing at page 243 of Hansard for that year, in which he said:
I wish this government could put every ablebodied man to work to-morrow, and I am quite sure that desire is shared by every member of the government. However I cannot advocate such a policy because I do not believe public employment through a vast scheme of public works is anything more than a palliative for our present economic ills. I believe that ultimately it would create far greater economic distress than that which now exists.
The minister himself is definitely on record,
I admit, as being opposed to public employment. But may I say to him that if the unemployed of this country are thinking in terms of public employment it is because they were led to expect such public employment by the government of which the minister is now a member. Let me quote from the speech made by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the House of Commons on February 27, 1933, at which time it will be remembered that he outlined the new Liberal platform. He said:
The Liberal party believes unemployment is Canada's most urgent national problem.
I submit that this statement is still true, although the right hon. gentleman has been in office for the last four years. Then he goes on to say how they would deal with this urgent national problem, and he divides it info two parts, how they would deal with the emergency condition and how they would deal with the long term problem:
It would deal with the present emergent conditions through a representative national commission which would cooperate with the provinces and municipalities in the administration of unemployment relief, and in an endeavour to provide work for the unemployed.
If I may stop just there, two things were suggested. The first was a national employment commission to administer relief along with the provinces and municipalities. Well, we got a national employment commission but it never administered relief; "it never had power to administer relief or to administer anything. It was an advisory commission that drew up a report at considerable cost to the Canadian taxpayer, and filed the report with the government, and then the members of the commission joined the ranks of the unemployed. The second feature was:
. . . and in an endeavour to provide work for the unemployed.
In 1935 from one end of Canada to the other we heard of a work and wages program. That was what the unemployed were led to expect. The minister need not stand up peevishly now and say all we can think of is employment in terms of public work. The people have been led to think in terms of public employment when private employment was not forthcoming.
Personally I cannot share the minister's great fear of public employment. I agree that it is only a palliative, but it is something; and when private employment is not forthcoming it seems to me the next best thing. Whenever I had opportunity during the last two or three summers I watched

work being done in the United States under the works progress administration in the state of Illinois and out through the western states. I have seen them take schoolhouses very much like some we have on the prairies now, unfit for human habitation, tear them down and build new ones; put in new town halls; asphalt the streets of their small towns and villages; pull down old homes; take burned out areas of land in North Dakota and Montana, irrigate them, move farmers back on the land and build houses and barns for them. They have taken their unemployed and placed them on little five-acre units with a new house, twenty-five chickens and a cow. They have guaranteed those people ten days work a month, which gives them enough money to buy their groceries. With their five acres of irrigated land they have their potatoes and other vegetables, and feed for their cow and chickens. It is not an ultimate solution, but they are doing something, and they are rebuilding the morale of their people.
I have no doubt the minister has visited the CCC camps, which, again, are public employment, I grant. But here are young men working, young men who are healthy, young men who are under able supervision. These camps are not perfect; some things will have to be done and some changes are being made. You see these young men cutting stone, planting trees and working at irrigation systems. They are working and receiving wages. Part of the time they get training. Above all, they are getting what the minister mentioned the other day, namely a balanced diet and proper supervision. They have a placement scheme to help these young men when they come out of the camps, and they are not allowed to stay on the labour market.
The complaint may be made that a great deal of money is being spent and that they are going into debt. But I do say that the United States is building up national assets, not only in terms of great dams, not only in terms of state assets, but in terms of a revitalized youth, people who are getting back their self-respect and their spirit of independence.

The Conservative party if it is to survive must draw up a platform embodying the principles he set forth, said Doctor Manion. "We need a platform, not drawn up by one or two men but by some kind of a convention."
"Let the members of the Conservative party once again dedicate themselves to Canada by guarding our freedom, but continuing to advance by avoiding half-baked theories such as communism, fascism and social credit," he said. "Let us build a great nation and not a conglomeration of antagonistic groups."
The Conservative and Liberal parties have been in power since confederation. They have presented platform after platform to the people. Year after year, session after session, parliament after parliament, they have promised the people that they would get the best brains possible to deal with this problem. What is the result? Just look at the mess in which we find ourselves in Canada to-day. I do not see how the Conservative party can feel very proud of its past record. I do not think the Canadian people are going to be fooled by a new man although he claims to know a good deal more than the hon. member for Calgary East. My hon. friend from Macleod says that we should send Mr. Bennett a wire. I believe that would be a good idea. After hearing the speeches made toy members of the Conservative party, I believe they should send the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett a wire, saying, "Come home, all is forgiven." What is the cause of unemployment? What is the cause of the economic distress that we have in this country? Upon what are we going to blame these things? That is the question I ask of the Minister of Labour.
Our economic system is divided into two main parts, production and distribution. The real purpose of our economic system is to produce and distribute. When we analyse these factors, what do we find? We find that neither production nor distribution is working favourably to the welfare of this country. We cannot blame the collapse of our economic system upon the elements of nature. We cannot blame the lack of production or the lack of real wealth upon insufficiency of natural resources; we have an abundance of natural resources in this country. We have all the building material and all the labour required to build fine homes; we have, I repeat, abundance of natural resources; no nation on earth is blessed with more natural resources per capita than Canada, so we cannot blame our economic distress upon unfavourable elements of nature or lack of natural resources.
What then is another factor in production? We must have the knowledge of how to apply labour to the natural resources in order to produce the goods required. If you had a modem factory in the heart of Africa and all the gold in the world you could not produce anything by using slave labour. Your
2932	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
people must have a knowledge of the technique of production. In Canada we cannot blame our economic distress upon lack of knowledge of production. The men of this country are willing to work, but we have machines that have displaced men; we have solar energy which has done away with the need for human power, so we cannot blame unemployment upon want of energy, whether human energy or machine power, to apply to our natural resources in order to supply the requirements of our people.
Then what other factors do we need? Money is needed. But those who have money to-day are afraid to invest it in the production of new wealth, for they know that they could not sell the goods; so they say, "What is the use of investing money in new production when we cannot sell what is already produced?" There is one flaw in the economic system, the fear on the part of those who control money to invest it in production because they know that the world over there is an unsalable surplus of commodities; the great masses of the people the world over are unable to buy the products of industry. There is the flaw-the money system.
Dealing with distribution, can we blame the failure to distribute goods upon inability to communicate our desires from one section of the country to another or from one nation to another? We have developed lines of communication that are quick and ample to meet all the needs of the present economic system. We can communicate all our desires for goods or services; there are plenty of communication facilities. So we cannot blame our failure to distribute wealth upon lack of efficient communication. We have a system of transportation, so we cannot blame our inability to distribute the wealth of this country upon insufficient transportation facilities. Compare our present facilities with those in operation away back in the early days when the Phoenician traders were trading all round the Mediterranean, using camel caravans and communication by runners. We cannot blame our inability to distribute goods upon our transportation system.
What then are we to blame? Can we blame our system of weights and measures? No, we have an honest and efficient system of weights and measures. When a man goes to the store for a pound of butter, the storekeeper never says he has run out of pounds. When the housewife goes to buy a yard of goods, she is never told, "We have run out of yards."
But the people who want the goods continually run out of money. That is another essential factor in the distribution of goods,

we must have a medium of exchange. That is what has broken down; that is the flaw in the system of distribution-lack of a medium of exchange in sufficient quantity to transfer the goods and services produced in this country from one person to another. There is not sufficient purchasing power in the hands of the people to buy the goods and services that we are capable of producing. That is why I say that our present financial institutions are Canadas public enemy No. 1; they are the subversive elements that are destroying the economic life of this country, producing ruin and chaos, creating unemployment and all the rest of the inequalities from which the people are suffering.
Now we, the party I represent, are not the only ones who claim that the money system is responsible for all the suffering of mankind. Let me refer to the evidence that was given before the banking and commerce committee of the United States senate by Robert L. Owen, former chairman of the committee on banking and currency in the republic to the south. He is associated with a group of leading professors, economists, bankers and industrialists in the United States in an endeavour to reform the monetary system. This is what he says, as found on page 52 of the booklet entitled, National Economy and the Banking System of the United States:
The contraction of the money supply not only increases business failures and decreases individual and government income but results in throwing millions of people out of employment, compelling the government to resort to various measures of relief and the expenditure of public funds on a colossal scale in order to protect the people from actual starvation and physical deterioration.

Let me quote Senator Wagner in discussing relief-and this sounds a good deal different from the statements of hon. members on the Liberal side:
On June 17 Senator Wagner said to Senator Bailey in discussing relief-
I have listened to the claims of the senator from North Carolina that there is no serious unemployment problem to-day. Does he not know that the very lowest current estimate of unemployment, that of the conservative national industrial conference board, is 7,533,000, and that the average of all responsible estimates is about 9,000,000?
What, in the senator's judgment, has become of the "technologically" unemployed? He must, indeed, be familiar with the tobacco industry. Nineteen hundred and thirty-six was a banner year for that industry.
He goes on to prove that technological unemployment is here to stay and industry is displacing more and more men by the use of solar energy in place of man power. And Senator Bone said:
The advance of technology in agriculture has tended to widen the gap in general wellbeing between farmers who are able to embrace it and those who are unable to utilize the fruits of science and invention. This gap is

certain to widen .	.	. the man with the
hoe and the man with the tractor are not competitive equals where they are engaged in the same type of farming.
In Canada we hear from the Liberal party, "Put men back on the farm." Well, here we have unemployed men who are willing and anxious to work in our large factories manufacturing farm implements, factories that are working only twenty-five per cent of total productive capacity. That is the situation. We can mechanize our Canadian agriculture and then we do not need the farmer; when that happens we do away with a field of employment which the minister mentioned this afternoon. I asked him what fields were open to single transient unemployed, what industry offered them opportunity, and he said, "agriculture." If we could put to use the labour and materials available for employment in our factories we could mechanize the farms of Canada, and then that industry would be closed to those seeking employment. But the Minister of Labour believes that the only way in which a man can make a living is to work, and if a man does not work he will starve. We have robbed men of the right to work by substituting the machine, and now we rob men of the right to live by taking away their wages.
The leader of t'he opposition said that we had only a half-baked theory. If I could get one half-ibaked idea from the Conservative party I would be tickled to death. He referred to the Social Credit party as being out to print unlimited quantities of money. May I refer to a gentleman iwho has made a greater contribution to the world than the hon. member will ever make, a man who is recognized as one of the greatest inventors the world has ever known-Thomas Edison. What does he say? What are his views on matters of this kind? The leader of the opposition did not give me an answer to the question I asked as to what was the value of money. Let me read to him what Edison said:
The only dynamite that works in this country is the dynamite of a sound idea. I think we are getting a sound idea on the money question. The people have an instinct which tells them that something is wrong and that the wrong somehow centres in money.
Don't allow them to confuse you with the cry of "paper money." The danger of paper money is precisely the danger of gold-if you get too much it is no good. There is just one rule for money and that is to have enough to carry all the legitimate trade that is waiting to move. Too little and too much are both bad. But enough to move trade, enough to prevent stagnation on the one hand, not enough to permit speculation on the other hand, is the proper ratio.

If our nation can issue a dollar bond it can issue a dollar bill. The element that makes the bond good makes the bill good also. The difference between the bond and the bill is that the bond lets money brokers collect twice the amount of the bond and an additional 20 per cent interest, whereas the currency pays nobody but those who contribute directly in some useful way.
It is absurd to say that our country can issue $30,000,000 in bonds and not $30,000,000 in currency. Both are promises to pay; but one promise fattens the usurer and the other helps the people.
It is the people who constitute the basis of government credit. Why then cannot the people have the benefit of their own gilt-edge credit by receiving non-interest-bearing currency, instead of bankers receiving the benefit of the people's credit in interest-bearing bonds? If the United States government will adopt this policy of increasing its national wealth without contributing to the interest collector-for the whole national debt is made up of interest charges-then you will see an era of progress and prosperity in this country such as could never have come otherwise.
The only function of money is to move goods. We hear Liberal members and Conservative members referring to " printing-press money " and to ourselves as " scrip teasers," when all money is just printed-paper money or figures in a book created by bankers out of nothing. Billions of dollars have been created by the banking system in Canada and the United States out of nothing-just fountain-pen money; bonds have been sold to the banking system, putting us in perpetual debt. When this matter is under discussion at a later date I intend to deal more fully with it, because there are a number of hon. members who still believe what bankers across this country are telling the people, that what they loan are the people's deposits; many people believe there is gold behind the currency, and currency behind the bank deposits. There are in this country many commodities of which we have a surplus. Consider the situation the world over. How about coffee in Brazil? How about corn and pigs in the United States? How about dried fruits and hides and wool in New Zealand? There are surpluses of commodities all over the world. The world conference of agricultural economists, in 1936 stated in their conclusions that you must increase the real purchasing power of the masses, you must decrease costs and enlarge the social services. Certainly there are surplus commodities in the world; yet in face of that fact the people are unable to secure them. There are people in Canada who want coal. We can produce all the coal that we require. There are people in this country who would like to eat fish. We have a surplus of fish which the people are unable to get. There are many who want radios but cannot get them. There are many who need medical and dental services and hospitalization but cannot afford them; these services are available in abundance, but people have not the money to pay for them. All we have to dio is to increase the purchasing power of the people and let them get more goods, and we shall not have to worry about our surpluses. I will quote a piece of poetry which I think will answer that objection:
Have you ever been to Crazy Town And walked down Looney Pike?
There are the queerest people there,
You never saw the like.
They make so much of automobiles,
Of foodstuffs, wheat and such That thousands of them do without, Because they have too much.
That is the situation. Surpluses should not bother us. I do not care how large your surpluses are so long as you are able to see to it that the people of this country have sufficient food, clothing and shelter.
I will not go further into this question at the present time. I will only plead with the government to. recognize that the cause of unemployment can be found in our obsolete money system, and if we are going to effect a solution of our problems we shall have to finance consumption. If the minister wishes to finance consumption through public works, in order to make people work for what they get, and not through a national dividend because he is afraid they won't work if they get the dividend, very well. We are in favour of the national dividend. But you as a government will not do anything. You will neither provide public works on a sufficient scale to solve the problem, nor will you finance consumption.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS-UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I have heard some very clever men say that a woman's tongue is hung in the middle and loose at both ends, but it seems to me that this has been refuted in the last few days. I have listened very carefully, very attentively, and in vain for a solution of this unemployment question. No one in this house is more vitally interested than I am in helping the youth of this country. I know what it is to bring up sons. I know what it is to see boys and girls helpless and idle. In this session, from my own small means I have given over one hundred dollars to men who have asked me for a little help. I have given eleven directed envelopes with the word "free" in the upper right-hand corner to men to whom I have given help, and have asked those men to whom I have given those envelopes and small amounts of money, if when they got to their destination, they would kindly let me know; in the envelope was enclosed a sheet of paper, and I asked each man if he had a pencil, and each man answered me, yes. I have not received in reply a single envelope or a single letter.
It is my opinion, from my experience during the last nine years, since the depression first struck this country, that there are a number of men-and I do not exclude the women- who under no circumstances would work if they could get along without working. But I do not believe these form the large majority. I think we are safe in saying that if they had an opportunity of being properly fed and properly looked after in order to be fit to undertake hard work, ninety per cent of our unemployed would go to work. I am hopeful of the young people of this country. For the last forty-one years I have been associated with perhaps twenty men to one woman, so I feel that I understand the male mentality about as well as anyone can. We have heard quotations from the Bible. I do not believe that when our Lord said, "The poor ye have always with you," he meant only poverty of goods, of money. I believe He included as well poverty of body, of soul, of mentality, of morale. We shall always have men and women unfit, by reason of their physical disabilities, to cope with the hardships of life. Unfortunately we shall always have men and women unable, by reason of their mental disabilities, to cope with the hardships of life. It is not always poverty of money that makes a man undersirable or that makes a woman incapable of fighting; it is poverty of many attributes.
I was afforded an opportunity of visiting unemployment camps in the states of Washington, Oregon and California. I have said in

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
this house previously that I believe in a semi-military training. I believe in disciplining children. My boys were just as disobedient, just as boyish, just as devilish as probably each of you men was in your youth, but I insisted that they show respect to their elders and that they obey. With that end in view I gave them a semi-military training, and I believe our youth should have that training to-day.
If we do not come to grips with this question, Mr. Chairman, we are sure to reap the whirlwind; there is no doubt about it.
I am afraid of a dictator; I am afraid of the brand of socialism, bolshevism, nazism, fascism, or whatever you may call it, that is preached in different camps, in different industrial plants, and taught from one end of this fair country to the other by men who want to make trouble. I shall be berated by many for saying this, but personally it is a matter of absolute indifference to me which party is in power. I want good government first, last and all the time. But whichever party you belong to, work day and night, honestly and conscientiously; try to do your best. I ask hon. members to my left, many of whom I admire, as well as others who, I think, become lost in the fury of their language, to consider the present and not to go back to 1930 or 1931 or 1936 or 1937. Instead of berating the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), who to many of us may be too academic or too dreamy, try to help that man do what you believe to be his duty, in the best interests of this country. That is what we are here for. I do not believe that by tearing words to tatters we are going to help the unemployed who are on our streets today; I cannot see it. Surely, as grown men, you are able to sit round the conference table and do what is best for this glorious dominion. I hear hon. members talk of our natural resources. The greatest national resource of any government in the world is the human resource; it is what each of us can do to help our fellow men. If anyone can tell me what I can do to help these boys who are walking our streets-some of them hopelessly gone, without a doubt, and others just waiting-I will crawl on my hands and knees to help them, because every time I see one of these boys I think, "There but for the grace of God goes one of mine."
Of course a woman of my age and with the experience I have had feels very deeply.- I am going to ask hon. members to discuss these questions as we would discuss such matters in the family. When your son comes to you in trouble you do not rant at him; jou do not pick up a book and say, "Here
is what so-and-so, a great statesman, had to say." You sit down and talk it over and say, "Son, be patient. I have gone through the same thing. Now see if you can't just wait, though it is hard to do." We must do something for the unemployed. The money will be found. With the state of the world at the present time, how can Canada, with only 11,000,000 people, buck the whole world? She cannot do it.
We talk about what the United States has done. Has any hon. member been to New York lately? In that city there are hundreds and thousands of men and women living in poverty, distress and filth. Yet think of the billions the United States has spent! Have any hon. members been in some of the other large United States cities? Well, the United States is an enormously rich country. She is our neighbour. I was born and brought up there myself. I love her. I love Canada. I love what Canada and the United States have both taught me. But I beg of you to forget, as much as you can, partisan politics, and to remember what this Canada of yours has come through, how well she has come through the tragedy of so many years, and to feel in your hearts that she is coming through even worse. You have it in your power. God knows that I hope we use that power to the best advantage.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the observations of other hon. members who have spoken on this subject. I am of opinion a great many valuable suggestions are before the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) for consideration. Of those suggestions I believe some may be better than others. After speaking to a number of business managers, managers of both large and small factories in my constituency, I have come to the conclusion that a great deal of unemployment can be traced to the trade treaties of 1935 and 1939.
In discussing conditions with those managers I have been told it was necessary for them to lay off a number of their employees. When I called on them in 1936 they told me that they were laying off a certain number of men and were shortening the hours of employment of their older employees. I returned and chatted with them in 1938 and 1939 and found the same circumstances.
I contend, therefore, that there is a great deal in the assertion that the trade treaties have caused unemployment in Canada. May I point out that a business man does not

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
accept excuses in connection with the running of his business. If he did that he would fail. Results, and only results, count.
Let us consider what results have been obtained from the legislation passed last year under the Department of Labour. It will be remembered that last year $80,000,000 was voted by parliament for municipal improvements and housing projects. Of that sum only $1,253,000 has been spent, or less than two per cent of the total amount. Can we call that a satisfactory result? Last year we voted $1,175,000 for youth training, and I believe that vote represented one of the best actions the government has taken. Of that amount, however, only $350,000 was spent, or approximately 25 per cent of the total amount. Is that a satisfactory result? Of
63,000	young people who received training of one kind or another last year, only 4,310 actually got jobs. Is that a satisfactory situation? Are we gaining anything? Are we going anywhere? How are we going to carry on? What is this government going to do if it cannot get better results from the suggestions made to it?
Its failure is not through any want of urging or through the lack of knowledge of statistics revealing the extent of the problem. Service clubs, business men, capital and youth have all sought to contribute plans and projects to help solve the problem. Yet, so far as the government is concerned, that problem remains with us.
I have a suggestion to make, and it is that the minister open up a campaign to purchase made-in-Canada goods. I believe if our people were asked to buy only made-in-Canada goods and not to buy goods the manufacture of other countries, many of our unemployed would receive work. I believe if it were not for the lopsided tariffs between Canada and the United States and the trade agreements which have been entered into, our factories would be able to operate almost on full-time, and thereby put to work large numbers of the unemployed.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS-UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to discuss this question of unemployment quite dispassionately and, I hope, in a tone which will in some way compare with that adopted by the hon, member for Yukon (Mrs. Black). I appreciate her remarks and the sentiments she expressed. I only hope each and every member in the house will come to a recognition of the fact that this problem of unemployment is a real and national one which must be grappled with in an altogether different manner from that which we have been using up to date.

I think most of us are in agreement with the fact that unemployment is still our most pressing problem. No great improvement, certainly no permanent or fundamental improvement has been shown in the last three or four years. At a meeting of the federation of mayors of municipalities held in March, 1938, the question of unemployment was seriously discussed. That discussion took place among a group of men who were in close and intimate contact with unemployment and the facts connected therewith. Those men knew what they were talking about. They knew it from first-hand information, and not from any theoretical understanding of the situation, or from any long-range view. After a serious discussion they considered and passed a resolution. This has already been drawn to the attention of the minister, but I should like to read it into the record. It reads: Unemployment Relief
Whereas there has been no marked abatement in the crisis of unemployment, which remains a continuing national emergency and national responsibility;
And whereas the terms of existing governmental agreements providing for the sharing of the costs of unemployment relief are unsatisfactory;
And whereas the resulting strain on municipal finances, due to the restricted taxation base available to municipalities, threaten the solvency of many Canadian municipalities;
Now therefore be it resolved:
By this conference of mayors representing all parts of the Dominion of Canada,
That pending the dominion government taking over, assuming and discharging the full responsibility in the matter of unemployment relief, the said government on the expiration of the present agreements with the respective provinces, enter into a new agreement with the provincial governments, whereby the dominion government assumes fifty per cent of the cost of unemployment relief, including medical assistance and hospitalization, conditioned upon the provinces assuming at least forty per cent of the said cost.
There is another resolution on unemployment relief reading:
Resolved: That, in recognition of the fact that unemployment relief, in one form or another, will continue to be a problem of greater or lesser magnitude, this conference of mayors urge upon the dominion government the necessity for continuing legislation which would place the administration of unemployment relief on a more stabilized basis than at present exists.
That is what came from that group in March, 1938. A year has passed since then, during which time these resolutions have been before the present government for consideration, but unfortunately no definite action has been taken. We have practically the same resolution before us to-day as has been adopted by this house at almost every session I have attended, and I understand similar

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
resolutions were adopted prior to the session of 1935. We have made no definite strides toward settling the fundamentals of this problem. I feel that a resolution which has been passed by a body of men who know this subject so intimately should receive more consideration than apparently it has been given. There should be not only consideration, but action by the government based upon the arguments put forth in the report of which this resolution formed a part.
Like every hon. member, I have been receiving many communications, not only from my own constituency but from other parts of Canada. I have received many copies of a telegram which apparently was repeated and sent from different parts of this country. No doubt this telegram has been inspired by some source, but I think it sets forth what the people of Canada are thinking about this national problem of unemployment. This telegram reads as follows:
Consider adequate action to solve unemployment essential this session.
My reply to each one of these messages has been that I am in complete agreement with the sentiment expressed and that regardless of what government may 'be in power, I am willing to do everything I possibly can to bring about a solution of this problem which in my estimation is so pressing and unsatisfactory at the present time. I feel that we must come to real grips with this problem, otherwise it will get beyond our ability to deal with it.
I was sorry to miss hearing the speech which was delivered in this house iby the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), but it was my privilege, while attempting to recuperate from a slight illness, to read it as it was quoted in the newspapers. I consider that was one of the finest efforts ever put forth in this house. I believe that speech contained one of the most valuable suggestions ever made for the solving of this unemployment problem. The hon. member presented fourteen points. They were not all new, in fact probably none of them was new. Some of them have been tried, at least in part, but I consider that those fourteen points should provide a good working basis for the solving of this serious and pressing problem. It is true the hon. member for Greenwood suggested that thousands had died as a result of this crisis, and while he did not give definite figures. I do not think any hon. member should expect him to do so. Death certificates are not made out in the terms used by the hon. member for Greenwood. Every hon. member knows, as I know, that there has been and that there will be a tremendous casualty
list in this and other countries as a direct result of the suffering which many people have had to undergo while this problem has remained unsolved.
I consider the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) has one of the most trying positions in the government of Canada. It is a position which I do not think many hon. members would care to occupy at this time. I have every sympathy with the minister, but I feel that if he had given the same attention to the fundamental issues of this problem as he gave to one of the statements made by the hon. member for Greenwood, he would have been able to come to this house with a promise of a solution which would have raised our hopes and the hopes of those who are in distress at the present time. The minister has admitted the great difficulty which he has experienced and is experiencing in obtaining one hundred per cent cooperation from all the provinces on any or all of the plans he has put forward. Some of us attach the blame for that to this government, while others attach the blame to various provincial governments. But no matter where the blame is to be attached, the fact is that the condition exists. I feel that each one of us should do our part in trying to remove that condition so that it will be possible to come properly to grips with this pressing problem.
Just the other day I was reading a few remarks by Mr. Purvis, who for a period of time was the head of the employment commission, the report of which we all refer to from time to time and consider to be of great value. Speaking about six weeks ago to a Montreal club, he used these words:
Too many units of government tackling the same problem along with all the overlapping, the unproductive bargaining, and the jockeying for places which inevitably results from such a position are reflected in what is rapidly becoming a stalemate.
That is a condition which actually exists; it is recognized iby the former head of the employment commission. It is apparently recognized by the Minister of Labour; it is a part of the problem to which we must give serious consideration, and it must be amended and rectified before the fundamentals of this problem can be effectively dealt with.
One of our most serious handicaps in solving this problem is political. It is unfortunate that the problem of unemployment, in which the suffering of human beings is involved, should become a political football or be dragged into the political arena for the gain of any party, provincial, dominion or municipal. I regret that it is in
2940	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
the political arena at the present time, and before I close my remarks I shall urge that an effort be made to remove it from the political arena and not allow it to enter dominion or provincial or municipal politics to be kicked around as a football between one party and another looking for advantage and trying to reach power on the misfortunes and suffering of their fellowmen. We see one government trying to get money advantage over another. We see provincial governments jealously guarding their so-called provincial rights. The job of solving the unemployment problem is in my estimation bigger than any right, provincial or dominion, and we should look at it from that point of view.	We should endeavour to
persuade those Who are interested in political affairs elsewhere than in the dominion that this problem will and must be entirely removed from the field of political operation as we understand the term political.
I have here some further remarks by Arthur B. Purvis speaking in the same address on the topic, "The Canadian Way." He said:
What is needed is the element of community service and self-sacrifice to add a mainspring to the efforts of the various communities.
Cooperation does not come automatically.
The national employment commission was a government instrument for securing nationwide cooperation, and when it was given a job to do it found no difficulty in obtaining a very wide community support across Canada.
The type of machinery needed now is one that should have the blessing of the dominion government. It should be voluntary and non-political in character, and it should be organized on a nation-wide basis with a common policy background. It should permit of the harnessing of local pride in local achievements.
In those sentiments Arthur B. Purvis recommended and urged that this problem be taken out of the political arena and placed in the hands of a commission that would be given the blessing of the dominion government. and they in cooperation with other citizens interested would goon see that the problem was removed from provincial and municipal politics so that it would be properly and effectively grappled with in a businesslike way without seeking political advantage for any group or organization.
Some of the plans put into effect within the last two years are good. But they are not sufficient and are not sufficiently pressed. We have had many plans put forward; this government has put forward certain plans and some of them have worked to advantage, more or less. But there has not been a sufficient number of these plans, and those that have been put into effect have not been sufficiently pressed so as to become as effective as they might have become if they had been
[Mt. Walsh.]
launched and inspired in a somewhat different atmosphere.
The question of public works naturally enters into the discussion. Is that a method to cope fundamentally with the problem of unemployment? In my opinion public works is not in any sense of the term a relief measure. It is a palliative, temporary, and quite frequently leading to results that are unexpected, and not in any way reaching the fundamentals of the problem. I am not in sympathy with a large program of public works, which creates temporary employment for a number of men, but when that program is completed they again find themselves on relief. If public works are undertaken at all they should, of course, give the maximum of manual labour and the minimum expenditure on materials. That view has already been put forward in this house, and I understand that the government, in laying their plans for public works, are keeping that in mind. But again I say a public works program is merely a temporary expedient, helping the immediate necessities of a certain number of people, but cannot be relied upon to touch the fundamentals of the problem. And it is the fundamentals that must be touched if we are properly to come to grips with a problem of such magnitude.
Youth training camps have been established by this government, and I would urge their further establishment, near large cities. Those who are in these training camps can be trained in certain lines of work for part of the time, and the rest of their time could be given to study, vocational guidance and other details of an educational program to fit them for further employment. If such camps were established near our large cities where so many of our young unemployed group themselves, they would be available-
